A further proposal is to renew communication styles and recruit staff skilled in both the internet and Marxist theory. Finally, they urge universities to occupy online opinion space through quality red websites, national legislation, and campus monitoring teams that analyse public opinion.

The authors conclude that universities must pay close attention to the new situation online. They should improve the mechanisms of ideological security and strengthen risk prevention, so as to train qualified builders and reliable successors for socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concrete example of how Chinese university ideological work was framed in 2017: its threat perception, its view of the internet and its practical measures.
quoteEn: If Marxism does not occupy the ideological front of universities, non-Marxist ideas will surely compete to occupy it.
quoteZh: 高校意识形态阵地，马克思主义不占领，非马克思主义思想观念定会争相占领。

glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping since 2012, centred on the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article treats ideological work as serving it.

A twelve-word set of values (such as prosperity, democracy, harmony, patriotism and integrity) promoted officially since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The authors propose it as the guide for campus culture.
Compulsory Marxism and Party-doctrine courses taught in Chinese universities. The article calls them the main channel of ideological education.

t: Is the neoliberal market mechanism an effective institutional arrangement?
st: A critique of Hayek's theory of spontaneous and extended order
zh: 新自由主义市场机制是有效的制度安排吗？
zhSub: 对哈耶克自发—扩展秩序理论的批判
paras: Zeng Xiankui asks whether the market mechanism that neoliberalism promotes is the most effective institutional arrangement. The article opens with the November 2016 Peking University debate between Lin Yifu and Zhang Weiying, in which Zhang described his views as the "Mises–Hayek paradigm". Zeng takes this as evidence that Austrian-school ideas still influence some Chinese scholars. The article argues that Hayek's theory of spontaneous and extended order, the core of his thought, contains fundamental errors. It concludes that socialist market economy is a more effective arrangement than the liberal market economy.

Zeng first notes that Hayek never gave a clear definition of spontaneous or extended order and that his terminology shifted over time. Zeng then identifies three flaws in the theory. The article closes with a section on how the critique bears on China's socialist market economy, the spread of neoliberal ideas in China, and the debate over supply-side structural reform. Its evidence includes trade institutions, the 2007 financial crisis, US inequality data, South Korea's industrial policy and China's growth record.

The first flaw, in Zeng's account, is that Hayek ignores how much of capitalist order is shaped by monopoly oligarchs and politicians. Zeng cites trade expansion tied to colonialism, post-war trade rules negotiated between states, the fate of the TPP and the power of multinational firms. The second flaw is that the theory cannot explain market failure. Zeng points to the capitalist contradiction between socialized production and private ownership, which produces cyclical crises. Zeng also cites rising inequality in the United States, including Piketty's findings, and argues that public ownership and state regulation under socialism control fluctuations better than Keynesianism does. The third flaw is that Hayek overlooks government regulation's capacity for self-adjustment through feedback. Zeng argues that South Korea and China caught up through the combined action of government and market, and that China's macro-control shows "constructive evolution".

Zeng concludes that Hayek's order was not purely the product of natural evolution, that neoliberal markets are not the only effective system, and that constructive rationality, including government intervention, can be efficient. The author calls for thorough critique of neoliberalism, which is said to threaten China's reforms. Zeng cites Xi Jinping's warning that supply-side structural reform must not become a copy of Western supply-side economics, and points to "shock therapy" in the Soviet bloc and IMF programmes as cautionary cases. The author also urges stronger confidence in China's path, theory and system. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist economist at CASS argued against Hayek and neoliberalism in 2017, and how that argument supported the case for the socialist market economy.
quoteEn: Hayek's theory of spontaneous and extended order contains fundamental theoretical errors, and the capitalist market system he champions did not, as a matter of historical fact, rest wholly on \"natural evolution\".
quoteZh: 哈耶克的自发—扩展秩序理论存在根本性的理论错误，他所推崇的资本主义市场体制在历史事实上并非完全依靠“自然演化”

glossary.explanation: An economic policy line announced by the Chinese leadership around 2015. It aims to adjust the structure of supply, for example by cutting overcapacity, and official statements distinguish it from Western supply-side economics.
The official name for China's economic system since the early 1990s. It combines market mechanisms with a leading role for public ownership and state macro-control.

Rapid market-oriented reform programmes of price liberalization and privatization, applied in the former Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in the early 1990s. Chinese critics often cite them as a failure of neoliberalism.

glossary.zh: 道路自信、理论自信和制度自信
glossary.pinyin: dàolù zìxìn, lǐlùn zìxìn hé zhìdù zìxìn
glossary.en: confidence in China's path, theory and system
glossary.literal: path confidence, theory confidence and institutional confidence
glossary.explanation: Three of the "Four-sphere Confidence" formulas (with cultural confidence) in Party discourse. They express confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics.

t: Enhancing national cultural soft power and cultural security
zh: 提升国家文化软实力与文化安全
paras: Writing in 2017, Yan Xu takes up the question of how China can safeguard its cultural security, defined as the condition in which a nation's spiritual culture, basic social institutions, symbolic systems, knowledge traditions and beliefs are free from erosion, damage or subversion. The article argues that cultural security is an integral part of national security and that, if the cultural and ideological defences are breached, other defences are hard to hold. Its answer is that China must build hard power and also raise its cultural soft power, so as to win what the author calls the decisive struggle for cultural security.

The article has two main parts. The first explains why cultural security is a major long-term strategic task and then lists the main threats and challenges now facing China. The second sets out how to maintain cultural security by raising soft power. The author draws on Marxist national theory, Xi Jinping's remarks on overall national security, US strategy documents, and examples from the Soviet collapse and the 'colour revolutions'.

Yan argues that cultural security bears on the survival of the nation, the security of the social system and the wider national security order, and that Western powers themselves treat culture and values as instruments of security and hegemony. The author names five threats: 'colour revolutions' attributed to Western powers; a 'political genetic modification project' aimed at senior politicians and intellectual elites; anti-mainstream cultural trends; negativity and corruption within the Party; and weak cultural innovation, marked by 'Western-style dogmatism' and academic corruption. The remedy is to raise soft power in three ways: strengthen the cultural appeal of Marxist belief, chiefly through Party conduct and attention to ordinary people's livelihoods; release cultural creativity by balancing politics and culture, market and government, and the 'main theme' and diversity; and widen the international influence of Chinese culture.

On the third point, Yan rejects the view that economic influence automatically becomes cultural influence, and calls for confidence in socialist culture and not only in traditional Chinese culture. The author also urges new methods of 'going global', since Confucius Institutes have spread quickly but struggle to 'take root'. This would combine government-led promotion with better marketing techniques learned from abroad. Read the original if you want to see how a Party journal in 2017 framed cultural security, ideology and soft power as parts of national security, and which threats it named.
quoteEn: Culture is the lifeblood of a nation; without the cohesion of national culture, a nation would be a heap of loose sand and might even perish.
quoteZh: 文化是民族的血脉，离开民族文化的凝聚，一个民族将是一盘散沙，甚至会消亡。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese adaptation of Joseph Nye's 'soft power', referring to a country's cultural appeal, creativity and influence. It became a prominent policy theme in Party documents from the late 2000s.
The protection of a nation's culture, values and ideology from external or internal erosion. It is treated in Chinese official discourse as one component of national security.
Term for the post-2000 regime changes in some post-Soviet and other states. Chinese official writing often describes them as externally engineered; the article follows that reading.

t: Contemporary Chinese literary and artistic workers must establish a correct view of history
zh: 当代中国文艺工作者要树立正确的历史观
source: Marxism Digest (マルクス主义文摘), 2017 no. 3
paras: Writing in 2017, Lu Guishan asks what historical task falls to Chinese writers and artists in an era of national revitalisation, and what view of history they need to carry it out. The author argues that a rejuvenation of the nation requires a literary renaissance. Writers must therefore chronicle China's modernisation and hold to a correct view of history.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the writer's mission in a time of social transformation and gives criteria for works that reach an artistic peak. The second turns to the creation of 'new socialist people' and surveys three kinds of subject matter that Lu considers especially successful: revolutionary war, science and technology, and agriculture. The third part, which gives the piece its title, names three mistaken views of history that writers should resist.

Lu draws on Engels's call for a fusion of ideological depth and 'consciously grasped historical content'. The author reads that content, for China today, as modernisation and the Chinese Dream of the rejuvenation of the nation. Writers should be both 'engineers of the soul' and 'secretaries of history' in the manner of Balzac and Tolstoy. Lu says too few works present the mainstream grand narrative, and calls for more portraits of entrepreneurs, builders and heroes who change the old environment through practice. Slogans such as 'going deep into life' are read as going into the practice of national rejuvenation. The three errors are historical nihilism, which Lu says attacks revolutionary heroes and 'de-revolutionises' history; a regressive view that idealises patriarchal agrarian life; and an illusory view that treats language revolution or 'aesthetic redemption' as a substitute for real social practice.

Lu concludes that scaling artistic heights depends on cultivating masters with ideals and conviction. In Lu's account they must be tempered by social change, nourished by the people and committed to refining their craft. The article quotes Marx on climbing the steep paths of science. It is a prescriptive statement of the official cultural line on literature, the 'main melody', heroes and historical nihilism. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist literary theorist links Engels, Mao's Yan'an Talks and the Chinese Dream to concrete demands on writers and critics.
quoteEn: This kind of fabricated writing, which seeks to achieve 'historical nihilism' through 'de-revolutionising' and 'de-heroising', has sunk into the mire of irrationalism and is the greatest betrayal of history.
quoteZh: 这种通过“去革命化”“去英雄化”，达到“历史虚无化”的胡编乱写，陷入了非理性主义的泥淖，是对历史的最大背叛。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese official and academic discourse for views seen as denying or distorting the Party's revolutionary history and its heroes. It is often used polemically against revisionist accounts of the past.
A slogan put forward by Xi Jinping in 2012 that stands for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and national prosperity.
A cultural-policy term for works that promote mainstream official values and a positive image of national development.
A phrase associated with Stalin and widely used in Chinese discourse for writers who shape people's moral and ideological outlook.

t: Literature and art must not be slaves of the market
zh: 文艺不能当市场的奴隶
paras: This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 12 March 2017, asks what goes wrong when cultural production chases ratings and box office. Hu Yinbin argues that literature and art must not become "slaves of the market" and that social benefit must take priority over economic benefit.

The piece starts from a report of remarks by a national political consultative conference member, He Xiangjiu, at the 2017 "two sessions". He said a private company proposed rewriting the script of the TV drama Jiao Yulu to downplay the "main melody" and add "human-interest" and "human-nature" scenes. Hu then discusses the spirit of Jiao Yulu, quotes Xi Jinping's talk at the forum on literature and art, and closes with remarks on how good works are made.

Hu reads the producer's demand as an invented, vulgarising treatment that dissolves the sublime and puts entertainment first. Hu does not reject portraying Jiao's human side, but holds that any such portrayal must stay tied to historical fact; otherwise it "lowers" a hero, distorts national values and weakens cohesion. Citing Xi Jinping, Hu says economic benefit must yield to social benefit, and that indicators such as ratings and box office should be neither ignored nor made absolute. Hu adds that art draws its life from the people and from close engagement with real life.

Hu concludes that a truthful Jiao Yulu, drawn from careful study, would hold an audience without invented drama. Works that move contemporary audiences need a sense of the era, historical responsibility and cultural mission, and a serious attitude to history and historical figures. Read the original if you want a brief example of how official commentary in 2017 applied Xi Jinping's line on art and the market to a specific dispute over a TV drama.
quoteEn: The people are the living source of literary and artistic creation; once art leaves the people, it becomes rootless duckweed, groaning without illness, a body without a soul.
quoteZh: 人民是文艺创作的源头活水，一旦离开人民，文艺就会变成无根的浮萍、无病的呻吟、无魂的躯壳。

glossary.explanation: A term for cultural works that convey officially endorsed values and themes, such as patriotism and socialist ideals.
Jiao Yulu was a county Party secretary in Henan in the 1960s, held up by the Party as a model of selfless, frugal public service. His 'spirit' is used in Party education as an ideal for officials.
The annual plenary meetings of the National People's Congress and the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, held together each March.
In cultural policy, the social and ideological impact of a work, which official doctrine says should take priority over its commercial return.

t: Key levers for building Marxist ideological discourse power under new conditions
zh: 新形势下建构马克思主义意识形态话语权的着力点
source: Studies on Marxism (马克思主义研究), 2017 no. 1
paras: Writing in a 2017 issue of Studies on Marxism, Li Jiangjing takes up the problem of how to hold and rebuild Marxist ideological discourse power (huayuquan) now that mobile media, microblogs and WeChat have merged with older media. In the author's account, this contest has become more concealed and complex. Li argues that it can be met only by combining institutional, theoretical and communicative measures.

The article has three main parts. The first deals with the interaction between institutional development and ideological change. The second covers three pressing questions about socialism with Chinese characteristics: the truth of Marxism, the originality of that path, and the moral and just character of its institutions. The third addresses how to raise the appeal of the mainstream discourse and use discourse power correctly. Li draws on Marx's 1859 Preface, the institutional economist Douglass North, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping.

Li holds that institutions and ideology evolve together and that reform must be gradual. The author recommends reforming specific institutions while keeping the basic socialist system, and warns against abrupt ideological breaks, citing the Soviet collapse. Li contends that Western countries, led by the United States, infiltrate Chinese thought and attack the Party's leadership. The author's reply is to affirm Marxism's truth, defend the originality of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and argue that Party leadership, people's democracy and rule of law are unified.

On communication, Li treats discourse power as "soft power" resting on academic discourse and on a basic mode of discourse. The author proposes building a philosophy and social science discourse system with Chinese characteristics, critically absorbing internet slang, and drawing on traditional and foreign culture. Li also praises Xi Jinping's plain phrasing, such as the Chinese Dream and "swatting flies and tigers together". Li adds that innovation must not distort Marxism's class standpoint. The author further calls for active agenda-setting and for refuting what the article calls false propositions, such as "revolution obstructs modernization" and "state capitalism". Read the original if you want to see how a 2017 Chinese ideological-work article links media change, academic discourse and institutional confidence.
quoteEn: We cannot only repeat the \"old language\"; we must also have a \"new language\" that embodies the content of the times.
quoteZh: 不能光说“老话”，更要有体现时代内涵的“新话”。

glossary.explanation: The capacity to shape how issues are framed and understood in public and academic debate. In Chinese ideological writing it is treated as a contested resource between Marxism and rival (especially Western) ideas.
The Party's official name for China's path, theory, system and culture since reform and opening up, associated with Deng Xiaoping.
A slogan popularised by Xi Jinping from 2012, linked to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

t: Four key points for holding the discourse power of ideological work
zh: 掌握意识形态工作话语权的四个着力点
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2017, Yao Dong asks how the Party can keep firm hold of the discourse power (huayuquan) of ideological work, which Xi Jinping has said must not be relinquished under any circumstances. The article argues that this requires effort in four areas: upholding and developing Marxism, building a discourse system with Chinese style, combining positive publicity with resistance to Western ideological hegemony, and strengthening ideological guidance on the internet.

The piece opens by citing Xi's speeches since the 18th Party Congress (2012) and the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016). The plenum stressed ideological and political building as the foundation of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The four sections that follow each pair a concrete priority with quotations from Xi and plenum documents, and each ends with practical tasks for Party organisations, officials and propaganda work.

On Marxism, Yao treats the Marxist worldview and method, together with Xi's governance ideas as the latest result of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context, as the core of discourse power. On discourse, Yao says China's development is often described by others through narratives such as the 'China threat' and 'neo-colonialism'. Yao therefore urges telling China's story in new concepts that are both distinctively Chinese and intelligible abroad, drawing on traditional, revolutionary and socialist culture while avoiding Western vocabulary for explaining the Chinese path. Yao also holds that currents such as historical nihilism, neoliberalism, democratic socialism, constitutional democracy, 'universal values' and civil society are tools of Western value change, and that they aim to steer China towards capitalism and must be openly opposed.

On the internet, which the article calls the main arena of struggle over public opinion and the 'biggest variable', Yao calls for consolidating the 'red zone', suppressing the 'black zone' and converting the 'grey zone'. Proposed measures include organised online forces, opinion leaders who identify with the mainstream ideology, stronger legislation and enforcement, and self-reliant core technology. Yao presents these as the means to make the Party's voice the loudest in cyberspace. Read the original if you want a compact statement of how Party commentary in 2017 framed ideological work, its named adversaries and its online strategy.
quoteEn: We must make clear the world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics: on one hand, it has broken the Western-centred model of development, ended the Western model's monopoly over global development, and truly shown the diversity of paths of human development;
quoteZh: 要讲清楚中国特色社会主义的世界意义，一方面在于它打破了以西方世界为中心的发展模式，改变了西方模式对全球发展的垄断局面，真正彰显出人类发展道路的多样性；

glossary.explanation: The capacity to define the terms in which issues are discussed and to have one's narrative accepted. In Party writing it is treated as a key resource in ideological contests, both at home and internationally.
The Party's work of shaping thought, propaganda, media and culture so as to consolidate Marxism's guiding position. It is treated as a core task of Party leadership.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan from the Xi Jinping era for tightening Party discipline, conduct and ideological education across all Party organisations.

glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context
glossary.explanation: The official idea that Marxism is applied to and developed through China's concrete conditions, producing theories such as Mao Zedong Thought and socialism with Chinese characteristics.

t: Putting Marxism and traditional Chinese culture in their proper places
zh: 摆正马克思主义和中国传统文化的位置
paras: Writing in Jilin Daily in February 2017, Chen Xianda takes up the revival of interest in traditional culture, in which Confucianism has again become a prominent field of study. Chen notes that some people now doubt whether Marxism still guides the ideological sphere, while extreme Confucian conservatives overstate their case. Chen rejects the view that upholding Marxism means belittling traditional culture, or that honouring tradition requires Marxism to step down, calling it theoretically wrong and practically harmful.

The commentary is short and organised around a phrase from the Classic of Poetry, "an old state with a new mission". Chen first sets out a historical argument about changes in social formation. Chen then contrasts the starting points of Marxism and Confucianism, and finally turns to what Marxism needs from traditional culture after the revolution and how that culture should be treated today.

Chen argues that China's revolution and socialist construction required Marxism because Marxism is a doctrine of revolution in the social formation. For over two thousand years, in Chen's account, dynastic changes took place within one social formation and Confucian orthodoxy persisted. Confucianism, based on kinship and the five human relationships, has no concept of class and aims to stabilise existing relations, while Marxism rests on class struggle. Chen also holds that Marxism cannot replace traditional culture. Citing Mao Zedong's call not to sever history, Chen says that after taking power the Party moved from attack to governance, and that Confucian wisdom on governance, moral education and harmony is useful for this. The pivot is "creative transformation", guided by Marxist theory and method. Confucius is to be restored as a cultural compiler, thinker and educator, and Confucianism is not to be used as a tool to justify hierarchy.

Chen concludes that traditional culture education must not replace Marxist education, and that the two can proceed side by side. Chen argues that students who lack basic Marxist concepts cannot observe the contemporary world, and that without them they will also struggle to grasp the essence of traditional culture. Chen calls for avoiding abstract, ahistorical contests over which of the two is superior. Chen opposes both cultural nihilism toward Confucian-led tradition and a conservatism that invokes tradition to attack Marxism and reject Western culture. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a senior Chinese Marxist philosopher framed the relationship between Marxism and Confucian tradition in 2017.
quoteEn: One is the theoretical guide of China's revolution and socialist construction; the other is the spiritual lifeblood and the cultural root of the Chinese nation.
quoteZh: 一个是中国革命和社会主义建设的思想理论指导，一个是中华民族的精神血脉和中华民族的文化之根。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist category for a society's overall type, such as feudal or socialist, defined by its economic base and superstructure. Chen uses it to argue that the move to socialism differs in kind from dynastic change.
A formula in Party discourse on traditional culture. It means reworking inherited elements so that they serve present needs. Chen treats it as the pivot for handling Marxism and tradition.

t: Choices of discourse in current ideological and theoretical propaganda
zh: 当前思想理论宣传的话语选择
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), 2017 no. 6, Meng Xianping and Wang Yonggui ask how the Party's ideas and theory can "take root" among ordinary people. Their answer is that propaganda work must build a discourse system and innovate its wording. They argue that failures of communication come from an unsuitable narrative mode, a badly chosen audience or too little identification between speaker and listener.

The article is a short commentary in two parts. The first part concerns the choice of discourse (wording, register and tone) and sets out three requirements: language that appeals to both refined and popular tastes, language that meets the needs of the masses, and language with a positive orientation. The second part concerns narrative form and sets out two requirements: forms close to everyday practice, and forms in which feeling and meaning interact. It closes with a warning against dogmatism and draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin throughout.

The authors contend that propaganda should move from theoretical narrative to life narrative and from abstract symbols to concrete ones, while keeping Marxism as the guiding ideology. They criticise propaganda that panders to vulgar tastes, trivialises theory or uses exaggerated, ambiguous or extreme language. In their account, "three vulgarities" language carries a bad value orientation and blurs the boundaries of Party theory. They hold that good discourse celebrates social progress and also criticises social ills in an objective way. It supports "letting a hundred flowers bloom" but does not endorse "fair competition" among all ideas. Citing Marx, they say that abuse alone cannot touch the substance of capitalist society. Lofty theory, they argue, must be carried by plain speech, and the sources of narrative should be sought in mass life.

The authors conclude that propaganda workers should give up dogmatic, formulaic or showy styles. In an age when everyone has a microphone, they say, official and popular narratives intermingle and crowd out dogmatic discourse. They call on propagandists to learn from the people and to present theory through lived reality, so that people truly believe, study, understand and use Marxism. Read the original if you want to see how a 2017 Party journal framed the style, tone and narrative of ideological work, including its use of classical Marxist citations and classical Chinese literary criticism.
quoteEn: Brilliant theory must be put into effect through plain language, and a rigorous system must be propagated in forms that the people enjoy and welcome.
quoteZh: 高明的理论要借助朴实的话语来贯彻，严谨的体系要通过人民群众喜闻乐见的形式来宣传。

glossary.explanation: An official label for content deemed vulgar, kitsch and low in taste. It has been used in Chinese media regulation since around 2009–2010.

t: No Party member may treat political discipline and political rules as a game
zh: 任何党员都不能拿政治纪律和政治规矩当儿戏
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2017, Yuan Xiuli takes up the question of why political discipline and political rules must be strictly upheld inside the Chinese Communist Party. The article argues that officials investigated since the 18th Party Congress (2012) commonly lost their awareness of these norms, and that corruption and breaches of political discipline tend to appear together. In Yuan's view, a defence line set only against corruption is one-sided and mistaken, because political failings can harm the Party as much as corruption, or more.

The article follows the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016), which restated that no Party member may treat political discipline and political rules as a game. It has two parts. The first explains why strict political discipline is extremely important, setting out four points: its primacy among Party disciplines, its content, the ban on crossing political red lines, and the regulations that support it. The second part sets out how Party members and organisations should put it into practice.

Yuan's central claim is that political discipline is the most important and fundamental of all Party disciplines, and the basis for observing the rest. Drawing on Xi Jinping, the article lists his "five musts" and "five never-allowed" acts, which cover upholding the authority of the central leadership, unity, procedure, obedience to organisational decisions, and the leaking of secrets or spreading of political rumours. Yuan cites Xi's warning that unenforced discipline creates a "broken window effect" and could reduce the Party to a "private club". The article presents newly revised regulations, including the Party discipline punishment regulations and the accountability regulations, as turning abstract requirements into concrete, enforceable rules.

For implementation, Yuan proposes strengthening education in ideals and convictions, since wavering belief is said to be the root of lapses. Yuan also calls for reverence for discipline and self-examination by members, and for Party organisations and discipline inspection bodies to take up their responsibility for enforcement and oversight. The article says that "iron discipline must be enforced with an iron hand", and cites expulsions of senior officials for forming cliques or publicly voicing views at odds with the Central Committee as proof that firm action deters violations. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2017 Party journal explained the official case for tighter political discipline and the content of the "five musts" and "five never-allowed" acts.
quoteEn: Political discipline is the most important discipline and the fundamental guarantee for safeguarding the Party's unity and solidarity.
quoteZh: 政治纪律是最重要的纪律，是维护党的团结统一的根本保证。

glossary.explanation: The set of Party rules requiring members to stay politically aligned with the Party Central Committee. Official texts treat it as the most basic of the Party's disciplines.
A term Xi Jinping emphasised from 2015 for the informal and formal norms of conduct expected inside the Party, used alongside political discipline.

glossary.pinyin: dǎng de shíbā jiè liù zhōngquánhuì
glossary.en: Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee
glossary.explanation: The October 2016 meeting of the Party Central Committee that adopted guidelines on political life in the Party and regulations on intra-Party supervision.

t: Two key points in advancing the popularization of Marxism
zh: 推进马克思主义大众化的两个关键点
paras: Writing in 2017, Zhou Xincheng asks what is needed to make Marxism accessible to the broad masses (Marxism's popularization, or dazhonghua). The article answers with two conditions: theorists and propagandists must firmly believe that Marxism's basic principles are correct, and those principles must be combined with Chinese realities to answer Chinese problems.

The piece opens with Xi Jinping's remarks on Marxism as the Party's guiding ideology. It then argues that Marxism has to be "instilled" in the masses because spontaneous struggles do not generate it. It rebuts a reading of the 1872 German preface to the Communist Manifesto, and closes with Mao Zedong's 1950s statements on general laws and national particularities.

Zhou names the main obstacle as theorists who do not believe in Marxism, reject its basic principles, or promote anti-Marxist ideas to the public. Against the claim that Marxism is partly right and partly wrong, Zhou reads the Manifesto preface as separating basic principles, which are the essence and remain valid, from specific conclusions drawn under particular historical conditions, which can become outdated. Citing the preface as proof that Marx and Engels admitted errors is called a deliberate distortion. Basic principles are held to be universal truths, yet they are useless unless applied to concrete national conditions; Zhou compares them to an arrow that must be shot at a target, and says copying foreign models must fail.

Zhou concludes that upholding the basic principles and developing Marxism are one task, since development means applying the principles to new situations. In present-day China, Zhou holds, upholding the theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics is upholding Marxism, so popularizing Marxism amounts to popularizing that theory among the masses. Read the original if you want a short, orthodox statement of how a Party-affiliated theorist in 2017 defended the universality of Marxism's basic principles against "partly right, partly wrong" readings.
quoteEn: It is like a good arrow: if it is only kept in the hand and played with, and never shot at the target, it will be of no use at all.
quoteZh: 它好比一把好箭，但老拿在手上把玩，不向“靶子”射出去，就会毫无用处。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's theory and path of socialism since reform and opening up. The article equates upholding it with upholding Marxism in China today.

t: Abandoning the communist ideal means abandoning Marxism
zh: 摒弃共产主义理想就不是马克思主义
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary (Jilin Daily, February 2017), Chen Xianda argues that no one who avoids the communist ideal can be a genuine Marxist. Citing Xi Jinping's repeated statements that communism is the Communist Party's highest ideal, Chen treats that ideal as the "calcium" that keeps a Marxist standing firm.

Chen begins with the problems he sees after reform: a widening wealth gap, official corruption, moral confusion and environmental damage. He identifies two opposed attitudes to communism: beneficiaries of unfair gain who fear the word, and discontented people who dismiss it as utopian. The article then separates three senses of communism, discusses welfare states, and turns to ideological education for young people and to the personal steadfastness required of Party members.

Chen's central distinction is between communism as a social formation (the advanced stage of socialism, still very distant), as an ideal and highest programme, and as "communist elements" present in current socialist practice. Policies such as common prosperity, poverty eradication and public welfare, in his reading, steadily add such elements to a socialist market economy that is not a "market society". Western welfare states, he argues, remain improved capitalism: taxes are accumulated surplus labour, and welfare ultimately stabilises the capitalist system. Without the communist goal, Chen says, the Party would merely drift, and reform would lose its direction and invite neoliberal interpretations.

Chen concludes that communist ideals should be taught to young people as part of their worldview, just as other social systems promote their own ideals, so that they understand socialism, capitalism and China's future. He holds that this is compatible with current policies, including private enterprise and wealth differences, because socialism with characteristics of China is a stage in a longer process. A firm Marxist, he says, must look beyond an individual lifespan and withstand the tests of money and status in the reform era. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a senior Chinese Marxist philosopher reconciles the communist ideal with market reform and ideological education.
quoteEn: A voyage without a destination is a voyage that can never reach shore.
quoteZh: 没有目标的航行是永远不能抵岸的航行。

glossary.explanation: A long-standing socialist goal of prosperity shared by all, rather than by a few, repeatedly stressed in Party policy.
The official term, adopted in the early 1990s, for China's economic system combining market allocation with public ownership and state guidance.

t: Choices of discourse in current ideological and theoretical propaganda
zh: 当前思想理论宣传的话语选择
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2017, Meng Xianping and Wang Yonggui ask how the Party's ideas and theories can "take root" among the public. Their answer is that this depends on building a discourse system and renewing propaganda language. The authors argue that propaganda has its own regularities and needs a suitable mode of narration, a sound vocabulary, effective strategies and a lively tone. Theory should move from "theoretical narrative" to "life narrative" and from abstract to concrete symbols, while Marxism keeps its guiding position.

The commentary has two parts. The first concerns the choice of discourse, which the authors say depends on the propagandist's theoretical training and style, the audience's knowledge and the social setting. It discusses three choices: language that appeals to both refined and popular tastes, language that meets the needs of the masses, and language with a positive orientation. The second part concerns narrative form and discusses closeness to everyday practice, the interplay of feeling and meaning, and the rejection of dogmatism.

Meng and Wang say propaganda language should embody truth, goodness and beauty, and avoid affectation. They criticise vulgar or comic styles that lower the persuasiveness of theory, as well as the "three vulgarities" (sansu), which they say carry a bad value orientation and blur the boundaries of ideas. They support "letting a hundred flowers bloom" but not "fair competition" among all ideas, and "a hundred schools of thought contending" but not nonsense. In the second part, citing Marx, Engels and Lenin, they argue that abstract theory must return to practice and be carried by plain language drawn from the masses' daily life. Emotive, concrete narration should rest on a clear people's standpoint.

The authors warn against propagandists who bluster, use stock phrases, or string together new terms without substance. They say such habits "sacrifice living Marxism", a phrase they quote from the classics. In the multimedia age, they note, official and popular narratives intertwine, which in their view crowds out the space for dogmatism. They conclude that dogmatism must be abandoned so that the true meaning of theory appears in the masses' real lives and people truly believe, study, understand and apply Marxism. Read the original if you want to see how a 2017 Party journal framed the style, tone and narrative of ideological work, and how it used classical Marxist citations for that purpose.
quoteEn: Brilliant theory must be carried out through plain language, and a rigorous system must be propagated in forms that the people enjoy and welcome.
quoteZh: 高明的理论要借助朴实的话语来贯彻，严谨的体系要通过人民群众喜闻乐见的形式来宣传。

glossary.explanation: A term used in official campaigns from around 2009–2010 for content seen as vulgar, kitsch and low-brow in media and culture. The authors use it for language that carries a bad value orientation.

A slogan associated with Mao Zedong's 1956 policy of encouraging varied artistic and scholarly expression, together with "a hundred schools of thought contend". The authors accept it within limits set by the Party's guiding ideology.

t: Ideological and political work must respond to the concerns of the times
zh: 思政工作要回应时代关切
source: Research on Ideological and Political Work (Sixiang zhengzhi gongzuo yanjiu), 2017 no. 3
paras: Writing in 2017, Zhu Lijia asks how ideological and political work (sizheng gongzuo) should adapt to the new stage of reform and development that began with the 18th Party Congress (2012). The author argues that such work can help build consensus on values, reform and development, and strengthen popular belief in socialism, but only if it responds to the concerns of the era. The piece is a short commentary published in a journal on ideological and political work.

The article is organised under three headings. The first treats the transformation of world civilisation under globalisation and informatisation. The second treats China's own social transformation. The third calls for ideological and political work to serve the building of a society of fairness and justice.

On the global level, Zhu describes a "civilisational predicament" in which material growth coexists with spiritual emptiness, and says that the neoliberal order is losing credibility. China's socialist success, in this account, strengthens its discursive power, so ideological and political work should "tell China's story well". It should do so by joining core socialist values with the "common values" of humanity. At home, Zhu points to interest differentiation, social stratification and pluralising values as the by-products of modernisation. These erode reform consensus and produce anxiety and a sense of value emptiness. The author therefore wants work that is targeted and differentiated, that strengthens the explanatory power of socialist theory, and that is willing to offer rational criticism of phenomena at odds with socialist principles.

Zhu concludes that ideological and political work should move beyond propaganda and education toward a "think-tank" orientation. It would study the relationship between values and institutions, assess the value implications of public policy, and embed socialist values in institutions and policies. People would then experience the superiority of the socialist system directly and come to hold socialist belief willingly. The author presents this as the route to long-term social stability. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar in 2017 framed the tasks of ideological and political work in terms of civilisational change, social stratification and institutional value-orientation.
quoteEn: Targeted, concrete, differentiated and individualised ideological and political work is the fundamental path to responding to the demands of the times and achieving effectiveness.
quoteZh: 具有针对性的、具体的、差异化和个性化的思政工作，是回应时代要求和实现有效性的根本路径。

glossary.explanation: The Party's work of political education, value guidance and mobilisation of the public, carried out in schools, workplaces and the media.
A twelve-word official formula of values (such as prosperity, democracy, equality and justice) promoted nationally since the 18th Party Congress.

t: Running universities well requires adherence to Marxism as guidance
zh: 办好高校必须坚持以马克思主义为指导
paras: This is an excerpt from a speech by Xi Jinping at the National Conference on Ideological and Political Work in Universities, reported in the People's Daily on 9 December 2016. Xi argues that China must follow its own path in higher education and that universities, as institutions led by the Party, must be guided by Marxism.

The excerpt moves from the strategic importance of higher education to the direction of Chinese universities, their core task of cultivating talent, and the content of ideological and political work. It ends with four points on how students should be guided to understand the world, their era's responsibilities and their own aspirations.

Xi states that China's distinctive history, culture and national conditions require it to run universities with Chinese characteristics that serve the people, the Party's governance, the socialist system and reform and opening up. He holds that the fundamental task of universities is to foster virtue and cultivate talent, and that a world-class university is one that produces first-class people. Running universities well means spreading Marxist theory, cultivating socialist core values, keeping campuses stable and building a good academic and school ethos. Ideological work, in his words, is fundamentally work with people and must centre on serving students.

Xi calls for students to be taught the historical inevitability of socialism with Chinese characteristics, to hold firm to communist ideals, and to link personal ambitions to the Chinese Dream and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. He presents this as the way to open a new phase for higher education. Read the original if you want a short, authoritative statement of the Party leadership's 2016 expectations for university ideological work.
quoteEn: Our universities are universities under the leadership of the Party, and they are universities with Chinese characteristics under socialism.
quoteZh: 我们的高校是党领导下的高校，是中国特色社会主义高校。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, closely associated with Xi Jinping's leadership.
The official name for the Party's path of socialist development since reform and opening up, combining state leadership with market mechanisms.
The policy of economic reform and engagement with the world launched in China in 1978.
A slogan popularised by Xi Jinping from 2012, referring to national rejuvenation and the well-being of the people.
A set of twelve official values, promoted since 2012, covering the state, society and the individual.

t: Building a new Great Wall against "spiritual colonization"
zh: 筑起反“精神殖民”的新长城
paras: Writing in 2016, Zheng Ruolin, a media professional who lived in France for over twenty years, asks whether China has escaped the "colonial and semi-colonial" condition in the spiritual sphere. The author acknowledges that China is now independent in military, political, economic and financial terms. Zheng argues, however, that Western "spiritual conquest" continues and that China is at the edge of being "spiritually colonized".

The piece opens with a short history of foreign domination since the Opium War and with everyday examples: foreign-sounding shop and housing names, admiration for emigration and marriage to foreigners, and hair dyeing. It then explains how this state arose, setting out its three features and the three "instruments" used to bring it about. It closes with a call to action. Zheng draws on personal anecdotes, such as a 1985 trip to France and a publisher who refused a contract because of the author's Chinese nationality, and recommends two books by Bian Qin.

Zheng says spiritual colonization has three features: treating the conqueror as spiritual master (for example, judging Chinese films and writers by the Oscars, Cannes or foreign literary prizes); willingly accepting the conqueror's power (for example, preferential treatment of foreigners, and weak Chinese influence on trade rules); and changing oneself to suit the conqueror's wishes (aesthetics, doubts about traditional Chinese medicine, "integration with international standards", wholesale Westernization). In Zheng's account the cause lies partly in China's own errors, as intellectuals after the 1980s took Western theory at face value, and partly in the nature of a Western civilization the author describes as monotheistic and therefore a "conquering civilization". Zheng names three tools: news reporting that fabricates reality, advertising that builds an idealised West, and cinema that redefines history. Zheng claims that over 90 per cent of French coverage of China is negative, against about 70 per cent positive coverage of France itself. The author also argues that Cannes selection since the late 1970s rewards films that portray China negatively.

Zheng concludes that China must build a new Great Wall in the mind, and that the first requirement is awakening to the reality of the threat. The author expresses optimism, pointing to China's five-thousand-year civilization and to a younger generation described as more open and more self-confident. Read the original if you want an example of Chinese cultural-nationalist writing on Western media, advertising and film, or if you study how this "spiritual colonization" argument was put to Party-oriented readers in 2016.
quoteEn: Today the time has come for us to build a new Great Wall out of spirit.
quoteZh: 今天，已经到了我们用精神构筑起新的长城的时候了。

t: Winning young people's hearts with the truth of Marxism
st: A profile of Professor Zhu Ling of Southwest Jiaotong University
zh: 《中国社会科学报》：用马克思主义真理赢得青年的心
paras: This is a newspaper profile, published in China Social Sciences Today in December 2016, of Zhu Ling, an 87-year-old specialist in the history of the Chinese revolution at Southwest Jiaotong University. It presents him as a model teacher of ideological and political theory courses. The piece opens with his visit to the Emei campus to explain the Long March spirit, where students and staff applauded him on entry.

The profile follows Zhu's career from his birth in 1929 and his studies in journalism at Yenching University, where he joined the Communist Party. It then covers his work at Xinhua News Agency and his posting to teach at the Tangshan Railway Institute, the predecessor of Southwest Jiaotong. Its sections cover his reform of the revolutionary history course, his lecturing style, and his mentoring of younger teachers.

The article reports that in the 1980s some students found theory courses abstract and dull. Zhu, in this account, neither criticised them nor enforced attendance. He consulted students and made the course useful by linking theory to practice, and it became one of the most popular on campus. His 'five-character method' (concise, practical, new, rational, emotional) is described, along with lecturing without notes and appealing to patriotism. Zhu is quoted as saying that such courses should open 'the window of the heart', not serve as a screwdriver for a toolbox.

The piece shows Zhu continuing after retirement to train young ideological and political education teachers, to supervise courses in Sichuan, and to give Party talks, including on the 18th Party Congress (2012) report. It offers him as an example of teaching that wins students through sincerity, expertise and care. Read the original if you want a short, official-media portrait of how an exemplary teacher of Party theory is presented to the public in China.
quoteEn: We must use the truth of Marxism to win the hearts of young people.
quoteZh: 要用马克思主义真理去赢得青年的心

t: Hot topics in the field of ideology and theory in 2016
zh: 2016年思想理论领域的热点问题
paras: This is an annual survey, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in early 2017, of the main topics debated in China's ideological and theoretical circles during 2016. Zhu and Wang report that the field "continued to improve" under the guidance of Xi Jinping's speeches on propaganda, ideology and culture. They identify nine "hot topics" on which scholars both studied official policy and argued against positions they regard as erroneous.

The nine topics are: studying the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016); the 95th anniversary of the Party's founding; supply-side structural reform; state-owned enterprise reform; the 80th anniversary of the Long March; ideological and political work in universities; historical nihilism; the crisis of Western democracy; and cyber security and building a strong cyberpower. Each section summarises what "scholars" affirm, then the "erroneous" views they rebut.

Across the sections, the authors present a recurring pattern. Scholars are said to treat the Plenum's naming of Xi as the "core" of the Party Central Committee as its most historic result, and to reject readings that they say loosen the Four Cardinal Principles. On supply-side reform, they are said to deny that it derives from Say's law or Western supply-side economics, and to insist on supply and demand as two sides of one coin. On state firms, they are said to refute claims of inefficiency, monopoly and "zombie" status, and to call for embedding Party organisations in corporate governance. On history, they are said to defend Mao Zedong and the Long March against historical nihilism, which they describe as a political current aimed at overthrowing Party leadership. They also describe the Beijing court rulings in the "Five Heroes of Langya Mountain" case as a lawful defence of heroes' reputations.

The final sections portray 2016's Western events, including Brexit and the US election, as evidence of structural defects in Western democracy. They also present the Cybersecurity Law and Xi's proposals on global internet governance as consistent with cyber sovereignty and openness. The survey concludes that scholars should hold to Marxist guidance, Party leadership and socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact record of the official line on contested ideological issues in 2016, and of which views were labelled as errors.
quoteEn: Supply and demand are like two sides of one coin and cannot be sharply separated; studying them artificially apart inevitably leads to confused thinking, with opposition and entanglement.
quoteZh: 供给和需求好比一枚硬币的两面，无法截然分开；人为地将二者分开研究，必然导致研究思路混乱，对立又纠结。

glossary.explanation: An official label for views that question or negate the Party's revolutionary history, its leaders or heroes. Party writers present it as a political current threatening Party leadership.
An economic policy line announced in 2015 to address overcapacity and mismatches between the structure of supply and demand. Chinese commentators distinguish it from Western supply-side economics.

glossary.zh: 以习近平同志为核心的党中央
glossary.pinyin: yǐ Xí Jìnpíng tóngzhì wéi héxīn de dǎngzhōngyāng
glossary.en: core of the Party Central Committee
glossary.explanation: A formulation formally adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee in 2016 to affirm Xi Jinping's central leadership position. The article calls it the Plenum's most historic result.

t: Four key points for firmly holding discourse power in ideological work
zh: 掌握意识形态工作话语权的四个着力点
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2017, Yao Dong takes up a directive repeated by Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012): the Party must keep discourse power in ideological work firmly in its own hands, under all circumstances. Citing the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016), which stressed ideological and political building as the foundation of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, Yao argues that this task should concentrate on four areas.

The commentary is organised as four numbered sections, each naming one focus and its role: upholding and developing Marxism as the essence and core; building a discourse system with Chinese style and Chinese flavour as the key link; combining positive publicity with resistance to Western ideological discourse hegemony as the firm policy; and strengthening ideological guidance on the internet as the key direction. Each section draws mainly on Xi Jinping's speeches and the Sixth Plenum documents.

In the first section, Yao holds that Marxism's worldview and methodology remain the foundation, and that Xi Jinping's speeches and new ideas on governance should form the core content of discourse building. The second section argues that China's development is often described by others through theories such as the "China threat" and "neo-colonialism". Yao therefore calls for telling China's story through new concepts that suit China and can also be understood abroad, while avoiding the uncritical use of Western vocabulary to explain China's path. The third section pairs proactive positive publicity with criticism of historical nihilism, neoliberalism, democratic socialism, constitutional democracy, "universal values" and civil society. Yao describes these as tools of Western value penetration meant to turn China towards capitalism.

The fourth section treats the internet as the main battlefield of public opinion and the "greatest variable" for ideological work. Yao calls for consolidating the "red zone", suppressing the "black zone" and converting the "grey zone". The proposed means are organised online forces, opinion leaders aligned with mainstream ideology, stronger internet legislation and law enforcement, and indigenous core technology. Yao concludes that these measures would let the Party's voice dominate cyberspace. Read the original if you want to see how a 2017 Party journal presented the main lines of ideological work after the 18th Party Congress, including its framing of Western ideas and the internet.
quoteEn: We must make clear the world significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics: on the one hand, it breaks the West-centred model of development, ends the Western model's monopoly over global development, and truly shows the diversity of paths of human development.
quoteZh: 要讲清楚中国特色社会主义的世界意义，一方面在于它打破了以西方世界为中心的发展模式，改变了西方模式对全球发展的垄断局面，真正彰显出人类发展道路的多样性；

glossary.explanation: The capacity to set the terms, concepts and narratives in ideological and propaganda work. Party leaders have stressed since 2012 that it must remain under Party control.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A Party-building slogan prominent since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering discipline, anti-corruption and ideological and political building within the Party.

t: Strengthening leadership and discourse power in ideological work at universities
zh: 加强高校意识形态工作领导权和话语权
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in February 2017, Deng Xueyuan and Li Guoxing ask how universities, which they call the front line of the Party's ideological work, can make that work more effective under new conditions. They argue that universities must hold leadership and discourse power by keeping Marxism as the guiding ideology, cultivating core socialist values, mastering cyberspace and putting the people at the centre.

The short commentary follows a speech by Xi Jinping at the national conference on ideological and political work in universities. It is organised under four headings: Marxist guidance, core socialist values, online discourse power, and a people-centred stance.

On Marxist guidance, the authors call for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, building Marxist theory as a first-level discipline and tightening Party committee responsibility. Propaganda departments, Marxism schools and all other units are to act jointly as defenders of Marxist ideology. On values, they say globalisation and the market economy have diversified students' and teachers' outlooks, so core socialist values must enter textbooks, classrooms and campus life, with no space given to erroneous currents of thought. On the internet, they urge universities to use new media actively, monitor online information and fill the field with positive messages, taking initiative on questions of political principle.

Finally, the authors argue that ideological work must start from the real needs of staff, especially young teachers, and of students. They also call for unity of Party spirit and people's character, so that the Party's positions reflect the voices of the university community. Read the original if you want a compact example of how official guidance on university ideological work was presented to a Party-newspaper readership in 2017.
quoteEn: Universities are incubators of social thought; core socialist values should lead campus cultural trends while respecting differences and tolerating diversity.
quoteZh: 高校是社会思想的孵化器，以社会主义核心价值观引领校园文化思潮，尊重差异、包容多样

glossary.explanation: A twelve-word set of values (such as prosperity, democracy, harmony, freedom and patriotism) formally promoted since the 18th Party Congress in 2012. It is taught across schools and universities.
The Party's work of guiding thought, education, media and culture so that Marxism and official values prevail. It is treated as a core Party responsibility.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for fitting Marxist theory to China's conditions and to the present era. The article also adds a third element, popularisation (dazhonghua).

t: Online teaching in university ideological and political theory courses: current situation, causes and countermeasures
zh: 高校思想政治理论课网络教学的现状、原因及对策
source: School Party Building and Ideological Education, 2017 no. 1
paras: Zheng Jie and Liang Hong ask how well online teaching is working in China's university ideological and political theory courses (referred to as "sizheng courses") and how it can be improved. Their article, published in 2017, is an empirical study that moves from a survey of the current situation to its causes and then to remedies. The authors argue that online teaching is now part of the teaching system and is welcomed by teachers and students. In their reading it still delivers only middling results, because of weaknesses in teaching staff, resources, environment and operating mechanisms.

The study draws on questionnaires and key interviews at 30 universities: nine from the 985 and 211 groups, 15 ordinary undergraduate institutions and six vocational colleges. Of 700 questionnaires distributed, 671 were valid, from 225 teachers and 446 students. The article has three parts. The first describes four areas: general conditions, teachers' and students' attitudes, teaching content, and teaching platforms. The second discusses four causes. The third proposes four sets of optimisation strategies.

According to the survey figures the authors cite, most institutions have the technical conditions, but online teaching is recent and infrequent: 48.44% of teachers use it only occasionally. About half of teachers (52%) and students (54.26%) approve of it, yet 67.11% of teachers and 60.99% of students rate their satisfaction as merely 'average'. Rich online resources are seen as its main advantage, while 41.78% of teachers and 39.24% of students point to over-virtualised platforms. The authors trace the problems to the weakened leading role of teachers, whose authority is eroded by information overload and, in the article's account, by Western ideological infiltration through the internet. They also point to duplicated, poorly organised resources, uncontrolled security risks and an underdeveloped 'soft' cultural environment, and to rigid assessment and evaluation mechanisms.

The authors call for four sets of measures. Teachers should adopt equal, open and cooperative teaching ideas, improve their information literacy and manage students online. Resources should be screened for ideological soundness, integrated by level and category, and developed into model online courses and MOOCs. The hardware and cultural environment should be improved, including network ethics education and the regulation of online culture. Management, interaction, evaluation and feedback mechanisms should be built, with the university Party committee leading management. Read the original if you want survey data on how Chinese universities implemented online ideological and political courses around 2016, and how the field framed its problems and remedies.
quoteEn: While online teaching plays a positive role in enriching the content of ideological and political theory courses, it also brings multiple challenges for teachers, which weakens their leading role.
quoteZh: 网络教学在丰富思政课教学内容中发挥积极作用的同时，也为思政课教师带来了多元挑战，从而导致思政课教师主导作用的弱化。

glossary.explanation: Compulsory courses in Marxism, Chinese Communist Party theory, ethics and history taught to all Chinese university students. They are usually abbreviated as sizheng courses (思政课).
Massive open online courses. The Chinese term is a phonetic and semantic rendering of the English abbreviation.

t: On upholding the guiding position of Marxism
zh: 论坚持马克思主义指导地位
paras: Writing in 2016, Deng Chundong takes up Xi Jinping's repeated statement that upholding Marxism's guiding position is a fundamental question for philosophy and the social sciences, for Party building, and for the fate of the Party and country. Deng argues that this position is the basic reason for the Chinese Communist Party's achievements and the ideological guarantee of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Abandoning or weakening it, in the author's account, was the root cause of the Soviet and East European collapse.

The article has eight sections. It first traces China's modern history from the failed attempts at national salvation to the Party's success under Marxism, then examines the Soviet Union's fall. It next considers the scope of the guiding position, how to treat diverse and erroneous currents of thought, and seven contested questions of theory and history. It ends with the need to "integrate" Marxism with Chinese conditions and to use Xi's speeches to unify the Party's thinking.

Deng contends that Marxism is not only the Party's guiding thought but the country's mainstream ideology, covering state organs, social organisations and economic and cultural life, citing the Constitution's preamble. Non-Marxist ideas that do no harm may exist but must be guided by Marxism rather than compete with it on equal terms. Currents such as constitutional democracy, neoliberalism, universal values, civil society and consumerism are described as aiming to subvert Party leadership and must be criticised. Deng also sets out correct positions on the October Revolution, Soviet history, the causes of the Soviet collapse, the first thirty years of the People's Republic, reform and opening up, and the Marxist meaning of democracy, freedom and human rights. The author also warns against both ultra-"Left" and Right errors.

Deng proposes continuing the Sinicisation of Marxism through integration with China's present conditions, its fine traditional culture and the practice of the Party and state, along with "four distinctions" among kinds of theory. Deng calls for Xi Jinping's speeches, studied systematically through the "Two Studies, One Action" campaign, to unify the Party and educate the people, and to be applied against Western-style democracy, neoliberalism, populism and anarchism. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a senior Chinese Marxist institution defined ideological orthodoxy and its boundaries around 2016.
quoteEn: The guiding position of Marxism applies to the whole of China, to all of our national, social, economic and cultural life; Marxism is not only the Party's guiding ideology but the mainstream ideology of our country.
quoteZh: 马克思主义指导地位的适用范围是整个中国，是我们全部的国家、社会、经济、文化生活，马克思主义不仅是党的指导思想，而且是我们国家的主流意识形态。

glossary.explanation: The Party's long-standing formula for adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, history and culture, associated with Mao Zedong Thought and later theoretical systems.
A Party education campaign launched in 2016, asking members to study the Party constitution and Xi Jinping's speeches and to be qualified Party members.

t: The "clumsy performance" of historical nihilism
st: New features of the trend of historical nihilism in 2015
zh: 历史虚无主义的“蹩脚表现”
zhSub: 2015年历史虚无主义思潮的新特点
paras: Fan Jianxin and Long Bin examine what they see as the new features of historical nihilism in China in 2015 and argue for a firm response. Writing in People's Forum in early 2016, the authors contend that the trend is not an academic current but a political one, aimed at inciting the overthrow of the leadership of the Communist Party of China and of the socialist system.

The article first describes the trend's timing, content and tactics, and then its use of "academic packaging". It cites Xi Jinping's remarks on the collapse of the Soviet Union as a warning. A second part sets out three ways of fighting back, which the authors present as necessary.

On timing, the authors say that nihilists exploit anniversaries. In 2015, the 70th anniversary of victory in the War of Resistance against Japan, they claim, some praised Kuomintang figures such as Chiang Kai-shek and Zhang Lingfu while belittling Communist ones. On content, they say a magazine's September 2015 issue carried articles that undermined the Four-sphere Confidence, for instance by calling "one-party dictatorship" Mao Zedong's legacy. On tactics, they list attacks on the "Five Heroes of Langya Mountain", the use of fragmentary personal memoirs against collective national memory, praise of the Republican era, and more veiled insinuation and mockery. Under "academic freedom" and "value neutrality", the authors say, nihilists reinterpret Party history as a history of power struggles and replace Chinese political terms with Western ones. The authors conclude that the real aims are to deny the Party's right to rule, its governing capacity and its political character.

The authors call for opposition on three fronts. The first is to take the initiative: answer nihilist claims, set the agenda and firmly hold ideological leadership and discourse power. The second is a strengthened sense of responsibility for ideological "positions", citing media campaigns and essay contests. The third is strict Party discipline, citing the newly issued Regulations on Disciplinary Actions, which classify "groundless criticism of central decisions" and distorting Party or army history as violations of political discipline. The authors hold that tolerance of nihilism amounts to indulgence. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholars described and countered historical nihilism in 2015–16.
quoteEn: Looking through appearances to the essence, historical nihilism is by no means an academic trend, but a political one with a clear purpose.
quoteZh: 透过现象看本质,历史虚无主义绝不是什么学术思潮,而是一股有着明确目的的政治思潮。

glossary.explanation: In Party discourse, a label for views seen as denying or belittling the official account of modern Chinese and Communist Party history. The term has been used in official campaigns since the 2010s.
Confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. A fourth, confidence in culture, was added later, and the article uses the earlier three-part form.
The capacity to shape public debate and set the terms in which issues are discussed, a key theme in official ideological work.

t: Building ideological and institutional defences to strengthen the capacity to resist corruption and degeneration
zh: 筑牢思想和制度防线提升拒腐防变能力
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily after the Sixth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2016), Lü Weizhou asks how the Party can build clean politics and raise its members' ability to resist corruption. The commentary takes up the plenum's call to build "ideological and institutional defences" and to construct mechanisms that make officials unwilling, unable and afraid to be corrupt. Lü argues that this is essential for preserving the Party's vanguard character and purity, for restricting and supervising power, and for consolidating its governing position.

The piece has three parts. The first explains why the task is urgent, citing the persistence of abuse of power, bribery and rule-breaking among Party members despite the anti-corruption drive since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The second deals with the ideological defence through ideals and convictions, Party spirit and self-discipline. The third deals with the institutional defence through rules, supervision and checks on power.

Lü's central claim is that the two defences are complementary: ideology is the precondition and institutions are the safeguard. On the ideological side, the author contends that corrupt officials generally neglected theoretical study and let their convictions slip, so that the "not wanting to be corrupt" foundation collapsed. Leaders must therefore hold to Marxist belief, study basic theory and cultivate self-discipline. On the institutional side, Lü cites Deng Xiaoping on the fundamental importance of institutions and describes the effort to put power "in the cage of institutions" through a system of Party regulations with the Party Constitution at its core. The author also points to the plenum's stress on supervision, including the Regulations on Intra-Party Supervision, and on the principle that power must carry responsibility.

Lü concludes that comprehensive and rigorous Party self-governance is a complex systemic project requiring several measures at once. Only if the ideological and institutional defences work together, in Lü's view, can a lasting mechanism against corruption be built and the Party's political ecology be kept clean. This is presented as a political guarantee for the "two centenary goals" and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Party theorists framed the pairing of ideological education and rule-based discipline after the 2016 plenum.
quoteEn: Of the two lines of defence against corruption and degeneration, ideology is the precondition and institutions are the safeguard; only if the two are linked and coordinated can a truly comprehensive joint force form and the effect of rigour be fully realised.
quoteZh: 在拒腐防变的思想和制度双重防线中，思想是前提，制度是保障，两者只有相互衔接，协调配合，才能切实形成“全面”合力，充分发挥“从严”作用

glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping's leadership since around 2014, covering discipline, anti-corruption and Party-building. Official English renderings vary, including "full and rigorous self-governance of the Party".

glossary.pinyin: bù gǎn fǔ, bù néng fǔ, bù xiǎng fǔ
glossary.en: unwilling, unable and afraid to be corrupt
glossary.literal: dare not be corrupt, cannot be corrupt, do not want to be corrupt
glossary.explanation: A three-part formula for anti-corruption work: deterrence through punishment, prevention through institutions, and ideological conviction. The article stresses the second and third parts.
Goals of completing a moderately prosperous society by the Party's centenary (2021) and building a modern socialist country by the People's Republic's centenary (2049).

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A long-term national goal prominent in Party rhetoric, especially since Xi Jinping's 2012 formulation of the Chinese Dream.

t: Holding the main front of ideological work
st: Challenges to Marxist ideology and Xi Jinping's requirements since the 18th Party Congress
zh: 守好意识形态建设的主阵地
paras: Li Heliang and Gao Qingtao ask how the Party should safeguard the leading position of Marxist ideology as it faces mounting pressure. They argue that since reform and opening up, market-economy development has produced diverse interests, widening income gaps and competing currents of thought, and that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the challenges to mainstream ideology's cohesion, appeal and public acceptance have grown more severe. Their answer is that the Party must hold ideological leadership and discourse power firmly, as Xi Jinping has repeatedly demanded.

The article, published in 2016, has two parts. The first diagnoses four challenges: the ideological fallout of comprehensively deepening reform, the infiltration of capitalist ideology, information technology and new media, and shortcomings within the Party-led ideological system itself. The second surveys Xi's requirements for ideological work in four areas: the armed forces, universities, the internet, and propaganda and ideological work generally. Each area is supported by quotations from Xi's speeches in 2014 and after.

On the first challenge, the authors argue that reform has entered deep water, touching established interests and shaking some people's commitment to socialism. Those who feel they have gained too little may turn hostile to the Party and to Marxism, and failure to respond would erode ideological credibility and even the Party's governing position. On the second, they say capitalist infiltration is now largely invisible, presented as cultural dialogue and "universal values" and even packaged as what socialism needs. On the fourth, they say Party ideology has weak appeal, relies on political authority more than reasoned argument, promises more than it delivers, is slow to see ideological causes behind economic problems, and uses outdated methods of education.

The authors conclude that, although the mainstream of ideological life is healthy, negative currents and a wavering "middle ground" persist. They present Xi's demands as the response: absolute Party leadership over the military, Party leadership of universities and their ideological work, a firm hold on internet public opinion, and Party-led media that must "be surnamed Party". Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a 2016 Party-school-style analysis framed ideological security and Xi's guidance across the military, universities and the internet.
quoteEn: The capitalist struggle against socialism is no longer armed confrontation but a contest of ideas, and it appears under the guise of \"consolidating\" socialism.
quoteZh: 资本主义对社会主义的斗争，不再是武力的对抗，而是思想的较量，并且以“巩固”社会主义的面目出现

glossary.explanation: The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China in 1978.
The Party's claim to direct ideological and cultural work, drawing on Gramscian-influenced Chinese Marxist discourse; the article pairs it with discourse power (huàyǔquán).

t: University ideological and political theory courses should focus on building the classroom
zh: 高校思想政治理论课应狠抓课堂建设
paras: Writing in 2016, Li Yan takes up the question of how university ideological and political theory courses can do their job under current conditions. The starting point is the Party Central Committee's stress, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), on holding leadership, management, discourse power and initiative in ideological work. Li argues that these courses must therefore treat the classroom as a front line and press ahead with classroom building in three areas: teaching content, the online classroom and the teaching staff.

The commentary is organised in three sections. The first concerns content and urges teachers to teach a living Marxism. The second addresses the internet and how teachers and students can judge and select online information. The third deals with teachers as the main shapers of students' values, and proposes planning for their development.

On content, Li holds that abstract theory alienates students unless it is tied to real life.
