The article has three sections. The first treats the formula as marking both continuity with and transcendence of fine traditional Chinese culture. The second treats it as an expression of institutional confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics. The third draws out what it implies for cultivating and practising the values. The authors draw on Marxist principles about social being and social consciousness, on historical materialism, on classical Chinese sources, and on Party and state documents on moral construction from 1949 to 2006.

In the first section, the authors map the individual-level values (patriotism, dedication, integrity, friendship) onto ancient sayings from Guanzi, Confucius and the Book of Changes. They also map them onto the "five loves" of the 1949 Common Program, the 1982 Constitution, the 2001 civic morality outline and the 2006 "eight honours and eight disgraces". They say this lifts "personal virtue" into core values and upgrades tradition rather than copying it. In the second section, they read prosperity, democracy, civility and harmony as the state's virtue, and freedom, equality, justice and rule of law as the society's virtue. They contrast socialist democracy, which they say rests on public ownership and removes democracy's dependence on money, with Western capitalist democracy. In the third, they argue that virtue means conduct, so the values must be practised. They hold that morality is determined by the economic base, and that public ownership supplies the material foundation. They add that moral character is built gradually, and they cite Xi's image of buttoning the first button correctly. They also warn of confused or distorted values among some young people, citing blurred ideals, "entertainment above all" and the mocking of revolutionary figures.

The authors conclude that treating core values as virtue directs people to begin with private morality, uphold public morality and understand great virtue. They say this should make the values part of daily conduct and, in time, a lasting spiritual pillar and national character. They also expect this "great virtue" to lead world progress. Read the original if you want a close example of how Party-aligned scholarship in 2015 linked the core socialist values to traditional ethics and Marxist theory of morality, and to the task of educating young people.
quoteEn: Core values being a kind of virtue does not mean mechanically applying or copying traditional moral ideas.
quoteZh: 核心价值观是一种德，不是对传统道德理念的机械套用，照搬照抄

glossary.explanation: A set of 24 characters in twelve values at three levels: the state (prosperity, democracy, civility, harmony), society (freedom, equality, justice, rule of law) and the individual (patriotism, dedication, integrity, friendship). The Party formally set them out at the 18th Party Congress in 2012.
A code of socialist moral conduct promoted by Hu Jintao in March 2006. It pairs eight behaviours to be honoured with eight to be shunned.

t: The communist ideal as a powerful spiritual force for realizing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
zh: 共产主义理想是实现中华民族伟大复兴的强大精神力量
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2016 no. 4
paras: Writing in 2016, Xin and Tao ask what role the communist ideal has played in the history of the Communist Party of China and why it still matters for the national project. They argue that communism is a scientific doctrine, a social system and a real movement, not an empty vision. In their account, the ideal has been the Party's "spiritual pillar" in revolution, construction and reform, and is a source of strength for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

The article is organised chronologically in three parts: the New Democratic Revolution, socialist revolution and construction, and the period of reform and opening up. It draws on statements by Deng Xiaoping, Mao Zedong, Xi Jinping, Hu Qiaomu and the report to the 18th Party Congress (2012). It also cites the Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party and a 1972 passage by Arnold Toynbee on Chinese industrialization.

For the revolutionary period, the authors say the communist ideal gave rise to a series of revolutionary spirits, from the Red Boat spirit to the Xibaipo spirit, and sustained countless revolutionaries through episodes such as the Long March. For the Mao era, they argue the ideal supported the Korean War effort, the socialist transformation and an independent search for a Chinese road to socialism, described as a "second integration" of Marxism with Chinese conditions. It also drove mass enthusiasm in industrial construction, which they link to the Daqing and Lei Feng spirits. For the present, they argue that the "great struggle with many new historical characteristics" and the complexity of deepening reform require firm political conviction. They cite the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe as a warning, and they treat corruption among a minority of officials as beginning with wavering ideals.

The authors conclude that, because China is in the primary stage of socialism, which they call the initial phase of communism's first stage, all current striving points towards communism. They call the ideal the "code" of the Party's success and of national rejuvenation. They urge Party members to hold to it unwaveringly, resist erroneous currents and build confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a compact example of how mid-2010s Party scholarship tied communist belief to Party discipline and the historical narrative of revolution, construction and reform.
quoteEn: The communist ideal runs through the history of the Communist Party of China; it is the code of the Party's success and also the code of the Chinese nation's march towards rejuvenation.
quoteZh: 共产主义理想贯穿中国共产党历史，是中国共产党成功的密码，也是中华民族走向复兴的密码。

glossary.explanation: The official Party judgement, formalised in the 1980s, that China remains in an early and long phase of socialist development. The authors describe it as the initial phase of communism's first stage.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, prominent in official discourse since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
The official name for the Party's theory and path of socialism since reform and opening up began in 1978.
The policy launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping that introduced market-oriented economic reforms and opened China to foreign trade and investment.
Mao Zedong's term for the Chinese revolution from about 1919 to 1949, led by the Communist Party and aimed at national independence and people's liberation as a stage before socialism.

t: Defending heroes is defending our values
zh: 捍卫英雄就是捍卫我们的价值观
paras: Writing in Qiushi in 2016, Zhang Mingcang and Hong Chaoyin respond to what they describe as a deliberate campaign to slander revolutionary heroes. They cite attacks on the Five Heroes of Langya Mountain, Huang Jiguang, Qiu Shaoyun and Lei Feng, and say these attacks try to "disprove" heroic deeds and overturn their meaning. The authors argue that such claims distort history, confuse values and erode the spiritual foundation of national rejuvenation. In their view heroes must therefore be defended as a way of defending the country's values.

The article opens with Xi Jinping's call to revere, defend, learn from and care for heroes, and then has three parts. The first presents heroes as the backbone of the nation, as exemplars of progressive values, as spiritual coordinates of their age and as vanguards of national rejuvenation, with examples from ancient legend to the War of Resistance against Japan. The second sets out a Marxist view of heroes. The third turns to practical measures for defending heroes.

The core argument distinguishes honouring heroes from three things the authors say critics confuse it with. It is not the idealist "heroic view of history", because the heroes honoured come from the people and depend on them, and the authors cite Marx on great men and Mao Zedong's line that the masses are the true heroes. It is not a personality cult, which the authors define as deifying individuals, since heroes can be groups or nameless and are meant to be models that others can imitate. It is honouring heroic spirit, so the idea that heroes are obsolete is rejected.

The authors present "deconstructing heroes" as a political tactic. They say it denies the Communist Party's historical record, undermines socialist core values and shakes the Party's governing base. They point to the Soviet Union in the 1980s and 1990s, where they say mockery of heroes such as Zoya and Matrosov preceded the collapse of the Party and state. They call for education in historical materialism, for continuing the heroes' spirit in the new era and, where needed, for legal punishment of those who spread rumours against heroes. Read the original if you want a clear example of how official Party commentary of 2016 linked the defence of revolutionary heroes to ideological security and historical narrative.
quoteEn: Defending heroes is, in essence, defending the nation's lifeblood and genes, the country's ideological security and socialist core values.
quoteZh: 捍卫英雄，实质是捍卫民族的血脉基因，捍卫国家的意识形态安全，捍卫社会主义核心价值观。

glossary.explanation: A central slogan of Xi Jinping's leadership, referring to restoring China's strength and international standing after the "century of humiliation". It is closely tied to the Chinese Dream.
A set of 24 characters in twelve values, promoted officially since the 18th Party Congress (2012). They are set at the national, social and individual levels.
The view that history is driven mainly by great individuals. Marxist writers contrast it with historical materialism, in which the masses are the decisive force.
The deification of an individual leader above the masses, class and Party. The authors treat it as a product of an idealist view of history and as opposed to honouring heroes.
The authors' term for questioning or mocking the accounts of revolutionary heroes. They treat it as a political attack, not as scholarship.

t: The Communist Party of China's exploration of core socialist values
st: Three historical periods, from the new-democratic revolution to reform and opening up
zh: 中国共产党探索社会主义核心价值观的历程
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2015 no. 10
paras: How did the Communist Party of China arrive at the core socialist values it promotes today? Writing in 2015, Jiang traces the Party's long exploration of socialist values and argues that it was continuous across three historical periods. In Jiang's account, the Party first fixed a socialist value orientation, then deepened its understanding of core socialist values after 1949, and finally formulated and refined the core socialist values in the era of reform and opening up.

The article is organised chronologically in three sections. The first covers the new-democratic revolution, the second the period of socialist revolution and construction, and the third the reform period from the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978) onwards. It draws on writings by Li Dazhao, Yun Daiying and Mao Zedong, on Party congress documents, and on Party resolutions and state documents on moral and cultural construction.

For the revolutionary period, Jiang identifies three elements of the value orientation: Marxism and socialism as the Party's fundamental commitment, wholehearted service to the people as its purpose, and the goal of an independent, free, democratic, unified and prosperous new China. For the period after 1949, the author points to propaganda for Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought, and to moral education built around patriotism, collectivism and models such as the Iron Man (Wang Jinxi) spirit and the Lei Feng spirit, which Jiang says prepared the ground for later formulations. For the reform period, Jiang lists five strands: Marxist guidance, the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the national spirit and the spirit of the times, the socialist concept of honour and disgrace, and the core socialist value system. The Sixth Plenum of the 16th Central Committee (2006) first set out this value system, and the 18th Party Congress (2012) called for fostering the core socialist values through "three advocacies".

Jiang concludes that the Party now treats building the core socialist value system and fostering and practising core socialist values as a long-term strategic task of socialist cultural development. In the article's reading, this reflects the Party's "high degree of consciousness and confidence" in building a strong socialist cultural power and strengthening cultural soft power. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned historical account of how Party documents and campaigns from 1921 to 2012 are presented as stages leading to the core socialist values.
quoteEn: The value orientation of socialism ran through the whole course of the democratic revolution.
quoteZh: 社会主义的价值取向贯穿于整个民主革命过程的始终。

glossary.explanation: A set of values promoted by the Party-state, formally put forward at the 18th Party Congress (2012) in three 'advocacies' at the national, social and individual levels. It grew out of the earlier core socialist value system.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: A framework first set out in 2006, comprising Marxist guidance, the common ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the national spirit and the spirit of the times, and the socialist concept of honour and disgrace. The article treats it as the precursor of the core socialist values.
The Party's official name for its path of socialism since reform and opening up, associated with Deng Xiaoping's call in 1982 to build socialism along Chinese lines.

Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution led by the proletariat, from about 1919 to 1949, which was meant to complete the bourgeois-democratic revolution and prepare the transition to socialism.

glossary.en: socialist concept of honour and disgrace
glossary.literal: socialist view of honour and disgrace
glossary.explanation: A moral code of 'eight honours and eight disgraces', promoted from 2006 under Hu Jintao as the basic moral standard of socialist society.

t: The advanced nature of culture and its "yardsticks"
st: An analysis
zh: 文化的先进性及其“尺度”问题探析
paras: Is there such a thing as advanced and backward culture, or does each nation's culture simply have its own merits? Li Chunhua, in an article published in Guizhou Social Sciences in 2015, rejects cultural relativism, which the author says denies cultural development and the progress of human history. Li argues that the very concept of "advanced culture" logically implies backward, decadent and even reactionary cultures, and that the standard for telling them apart must be clarified.

The article first contrasts classical cultural evolutionism with cultural relativism in Western thought, then notes that Marxist classics never treated cultural advancement as a separate topic. Li credits the Communist Party of China with first putting forward the concept of "advanced culture", and describes the Chinese version as socialist culture guided by Marxism and oriented to modernization, the world and the future. The main body then examines four yardsticks in turn (rational, historical, material and value) before discussing how they combine.

Li's core claim is that advanced culture must be judged by the concrete, dialectical unity of these four. The rational yardstick demands scientific truthfulness and objectivity, and Li treats "Eurocentrism" and "universal values" as unscientific biases. The historical yardstick makes advancement relative to an era: traditional culture was once advanced. The material yardstick, which Li calls fundamental, rests on historical materialism and ties cultural progress to the development of the productive forces. Because material growth does not automatically raise cultural life, as Li says of alienation in the West and spiritual confusion in China since reform and opening up, a value yardstick is added: culture must serve people's liberation and all-round development.

Li concludes that when the yardsticks conflict, the historical yardstick takes priority. Religion, though unscientific, was once progressive; Confucian culture suppressed individuality but supported feudal stability and productive forces; contemporary capitalist culture, despite alienation, is judged more advanced than feudal culture. Li adds that the "people" is a historical category, as Mao Zedong's wartime anti-Japanese culture shows. Over the long run, advanced culture is said to reshape backward culture, so recognising historical progress means recognising cultural advancement. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar builds a multi-criteria framework for judging cultural advancement and handles cases that appear to contradict it.
quoteEn: The productive-forces standard is the fundamental standard, but not the only one.
quoteZh: 生产力标准是根本标准，但不是唯一的标准。

glossary.explanation: A concept the Communist Party of China put forward in the early 2000s, notably in the Three Represents. It denotes culture seen as fitting the needs of the era and promoting productive forces, social progress and human development.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world begun in China in 1978.

t: Lenin's defence and consolidation of the Party: the historical facts must not be distorted
zh: 列宁维护和巩固党的历史事实不容歪曲
paras: Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2016, Yuan Xiuli takes up the long-running criticism of the "Resolution on Party Unity" that Lenin drafted for the Tenth Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in March 1921. Critics, the author says, portray it as a product of factional struggle, a tool for crushing the opposition and defending one-party rule, and proof of Lenin's \"autocratic thinking\". Yuan argues that this reading fits neither Lenin's thought nor the historical facts, and that the resolution aimed to preserve Party unity and strengthen Party leadership in a crisis.

The article is a short commentary in three parts: safeguarding Party unity, consolidating Party leadership, and securing the most urgent task of economic construction. It relies mainly on Lenin's speeches and writings from the Tenth Congress, cited from the Chinese edition of his Collected Works, together with State and Revolution. It sets the resolution against the conditions of 1921: years of war, economic ruin, the Kronstadt rebellion of February and the shift to the New Economic Policy.

Yuan's central argument is that the resolution was a call for unity rather than an attack. In the author's account, it acknowledged the reasonable criticisms of the \"Workers' Opposition\", on bureaucracy, democracy and the removal of unreliable elements. The Congress also elected members of the Workers' Opposition and the Democratic Centralists to the Central Committee, and asked those who offered to resign to stay in post. Yuan holds that these groups nonetheless drifted into syndicalism and anarchism: they sought a congress of producers to run the economy, put trade unions above the Party and opposed the New Economic Policy from the \"left\". In Yuan's reading, Lenin therefore distinguished theoretical debate in journals and collections from factional organisation and public agitation. Under siege conditions, the author says, a prolonged debate over the role of the trade unions was a \"luxury\" that distracted the Party from economic recovery and threatened the dictatorship of the proletariat.

Yuan concludes that the resolution was needed in spring 1921. It settled the disagreements, kept the Party united, strengthened its leadership and kept socialist construction on course. The author adds that Lenin called the New Economic Policy an \"unprecedented retreat\" and that it demanded even firmer conviction, unity of thought and discipline than the civil war had. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Chinese Party commentary defends Lenin's 1921 ban on factions against the charge of authoritarianism.
quoteEn: Preserving the unity of the Party and achieving unity of will in the proletarian vanguard are the basic conditions for guaranteeing the victory of the dictatorship of the proletariat.
quoteZh: 保持党的统一和实现无产阶级先锋队意志的统一是保证无产阶级专政胜利的基本条件。

glossary.explanation: A faction in the Russian Communist Party around 1920–21, led by Alexander Shlyapnikov and Alexandra Kollontai. It demanded that trade unions and producers manage the economy and criticised bureaucracy in the Party.
Another oppositional group in the Russian Communist Party in 1920–21. It criticised the Party's bureaucratic centralisation and called for more internal democracy.
The policy adopted in Soviet Russia in 1921 that replaced grain requisition with a tax in kind and allowed limited private trade. It replaced the policies of War Communism.
A Marxist term for working-class political rule in the transition from capitalism to socialism. In the Leninist tradition it is exercised through the Communist Party.

t: Countering Western "internet freedom" requires safeguarding China's ideological security
zh: 应对西方“网络自由”必须维护我国意识形态安全
paras: Writing in Red Flag Digest in 2016, shortly after Xi Jinping's 19 April speech at a symposium on cybersecurity and informatization, Zhang Weiliang and He Qiujuan take up the place of ideological security within national cybersecurity. They argue that ideological security comes first online, and that the "internet freedom" promoted by the United States and other Western states is a cover for cyber hegemony and ideological export. In the authors' view, China must therefore uphold its socialist ideology and become a cyber power.

The commentary has four parts. It first describes "internet freedom" as the greatest threat to other countries' cybersecurity, then argues that cyber sovereignty is internationally recognised, so that "internet freedom" has no basis. It next sets out the concrete threats these ideas pose to China's online ideological security, and ends with measures to defend it.

The central argument is that "internet freedom" is a claim to "first-occupier sovereignty" backed by Western technological superiority, so it can only be freedom for the West. The authors point to double standards, citing the Snowden revelations and a US defence secretary's remark that cyber attacks are a means of containing hostile states. They say cyber sovereignty rests on the objective existence of cyberspace, on cyber frontiers and cyber defence, and on legal grounds such as the 2003 World Summit on the Information Society. Freedom without limits, they write, is merely a synonym for power politics, and Western states themselves recognise sovereignty when they build cyber defences and conduct surveillance. Domestically, the authors blame netizens swayed by "universal values", scholars who advocate constitutional democracy, Western-backed opinion leaders, commercial media and historical nihilism for weakening mainstream ideology.

The authors call for a long struggle on several fronts. They ask mainstream media to assert cyber sovereignty openly and to set an example for commercial outlets. They want core technologies developed so that China moves from a large to a strong cyber power, and cyber legislation strengthened following the Fourth Plenum of the 18th Central Committee. They also want netizens to gain media literacy and "immunity" through socialist core values, building a "psychological defence" alongside technical defence. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Party-journal commentary links cyber sovereignty, Western "internet freedom" and ideological security.
quoteEn: Without sovereignty, freedom is a empty claim.
quoteZh: 没有主权，自由就是妄言。

glossary.explanation: The principle that a state has authority over internet infrastructure, information and policy within its territory. Xi Jinping promoted it at the World Internet Conference in 2015.
The Chinese idea that the dominance and stability of the state's official ideology, here socialism and Marxism, is part of national security and must be protected from outside influence.
A twelve-term official set of values promoted from the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering the national, social and individual levels.
A term used in Party discourse for views that are said to deny or distort the official account of Chinese revolutionary and socialist history.
An official goal of becoming a leading state in internet technology, infrastructure and governance, not only in the number of users.

t: Relying on study to move towards the future: new practice in the collective study sessions of the Political Bureau since the 18th Party Congress
zh: 依靠学习走向未来—— 党的十八大以来中央政治局集体学习的新实践
paras: Published in Qiushi in April 2016, this commentary reviews the collective study sessions of the Political Bureau of the Central Committee since the 18th Party Congress (2012). It argues that, under Xi Jinping's leadership, these sessions have continued the Party's tradition of valuing study and have set an example for improving the Party's capacity to govern. Its central claim is that the Party, having reached the present through study, must also rely on study to reach the future.

The piece is organised in four parts. The first presents the sessions as a way of mastering the Party's core intellectual tools. The second treats study as a means of overcoming what Xi calls "skill panic". The third describes the methods of viewing the situation from a high vantage point, and the fourth presents study as a means of unifying thought and driving implementation. It draws on examples from specific sessions, including the first, the third, the fifteenth, the twenty-seventh and the thirtieth.

In the author's account, the sessions begin with the basic principles of Marxism: scientific socialism, historical and dialectical materialism, and political economy. These principles are said to underpin judgements on deepening reform, relying on the people and managing the economy. The author says study also meets the Party's "skill panic", summed up by Xi as new methods not known, old methods not working, hard methods not dared and soft methods not effective. Study is said to help leaders grasp the "way" (the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics), fill gaps in knowledge and improve decision-making. The article adds that the sessions link domestic and international affairs, connect history, present and future, and use the dialectic of priorities and the whole to identify strategic focal points for the 13th Five-Year Plan period. It cites sessions that turned Party Plenum decisions into guidance, such as on the market and government roles and on supply-side structural reform. The author also says the sessions favour practical action over empty talk, in the spirit of the "Three Stricts and Three Earnests".

The author concludes that all Party members should follow the Political Bureau's example and carry out the "Two Studies, One Action" campaign of study and education. The aim is to become qualified members who are politically committed, disciplined, moral and dedicated, and to contribute to upholding and developing socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Party journal presented the Political Bureau's study sessions as a model of leadership learning and policy implementation.
quoteEn: The whole purpose of study lies in application.
quoteZh: 学习的目的全在于应用。

glossary.explanation: A phrase used in Party discourse for the anxiety that cadres lack the skills needed to cope with new tasks. Xi Jinping summarised it as new methods not known, old methods not working, hard methods not dared and soft methods not effective.

glossary.en: collective study sessions of the Political Bureau
glossary.explanation: Regular sessions in which members of the Party's Political Bureau study a chosen topic together, led by invited experts. The practice dates back to the 1990s and is presented as setting an example for the whole Party.
A slogan from Xi Jinping (2014) for cadre conduct: be strict in self-cultivation, in using power and in self-discipline, and be earnest in planning, in work and in conduct.
A Party education campaign launched in 2016. Members study the Party constitution and Xi Jinping's speeches, and strive to be qualified Party members.
An economic policy line put forward by Xi Jinping in late 2015. Its priorities are cutting overcapacity, destocking, deleveraging, lowering costs and shoring up weak points.

t: Accurately grasping the new situation in the contest for ideological discourse power on the internet
zh: 准确把握互联网意识形态话语权争夺的新形势
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2015, no. 22), Li Jiangjing and Xu Hongye ask how Marxism can keep its guiding position in China's ideological sphere as the contest for ideological discourse power online takes new forms. They argue that this contest has shifted with advances in information technology. Winning it requires attention to the key links in how online discourse power is produced, to three new trends, and to specific points of leverage.

The article has three parts. The first identifies three critical nodes in the production of internet ideological discourse power: the subject's right of dissemination, the right to set topics, and the right to use discourse carriers. The second describes three new features of the contest. The third sets out where effort should be directed: theoretical innovation, control of capital and technology, and three concrete paths.

The authors treat dissemination as the precondition, because equal rights of expression online mean little for individuals who lack network resources, so large media still hold the advantage. Topic-setting is the pivot, illustrated by the 2015 debate on Western values in universities and the Qing'an police shooting incident, both said to have been framed to steer opinion against the government. Control of carriers is the foundation. Citing the 2013 'Prism' revelations, ICANN's link to the US Commerce Department, root-server control and the market dominance of firms such as Microsoft and Intel, the authors claim that the US exerts technological hegemony and infiltrates Chinese opinion. The new trends they identify are a move from holding platforms to seizing topics, from spontaneous ('in-itself') to conscious ('for-itself') non-mainstream ideologies that attack heroes and revolutionary history, and from complete narratives to fragmented dissemination, such as altered headlines and 'big V' reposting.

The authors conclude that the basic task is to spread innovative theory that combines Marxism with Chinese realities, and to answer the problems China faces. They also call for control over capital, to counter discourse monopoly by internet firms, and for developing China's own core technology. Their three paths are to renew the forms of expression while keeping Marxism's core discourse, to take the initiative in agenda-setting through mainstream media and cultivated opinion leaders, and to innovate in communication. The last path combines united-front work with struggle, and debate with hostile forces. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese ideological-work scholarship framed online opinion contests and cyber-sovereignty in 2015.
quoteEn: Holding the right to set topics online allows one to influence opinion by supplying information and arranging meaning, shaping what people think about and how they think, and it is the pivotal link in realising internet ideological discourse power.
quoteZh: 拥有网络话语主题设置权，可以通过提供信息和安排意义来影响舆论，左右人们“想什么”、“怎样想”，是互联网意识形态话语权实现的枢纽环节。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese ideological-work scholarship for the capacity to shape public opinion and values through speech and communication. It covers who gets heard and whose framing prevails.
The officially promoted ideology, centred on Marxism and socialism with Chinese characteristics, as opposed to what Chinese writers call non-mainstream ideologies.
A communication-studies concept referring to media's ability to determine which issues the public regards as important. The authors apply it to online topic framing.
Slang for influential social-media users with verified accounts and large followings, often critical commentators.

t: Holding fast to the Communist Party of China's Marxist conception
zh: 坚守中国共产党的马克思主义理念
paras: Writing in 2016, Mei Rongzheng argues that China's ideological sphere is marked by fierce disputes in which historical nihilism, neoliberalism, democratic socialism, "universal values" and Western constitutional democracy are aimed at the Party's guiding ideology. In Mei's account, these currents try to negate individual Marxist principles and also to wreck Marxism as a whole. The article's answer is that their methods can be identified and that the Party must hold firmly to its own Marxist conception.

The piece has two parts. The first lists ten techniques used against Marxism, including altering propositions, distorting original meaning, dismembering the system, over-extending concepts, attacking the essence, coining false terms and subverting institutions. Mei analyses six of them with examples. The second part sets out three ways of responding to what the author calls noise and discordant voices.

Mei's examples are meant to show deliberate manipulation. Changing "ultimate" to "sole" in the claim that productive forces determine social development, Mei says, turns historical materialism into a crude productive-forces thesis and undermines the Party's basic line. Reading the Communist Manifesto as abolishing all personal property, Mei argues, ignores that it targets private ownership of the means of production. The author also contends that Marxism is split vertically, by setting the periods before and after reform and opening up against each other, and horizontally, into "ecological", "organic" or "feminist" Marxisms. Treating every critic of capitalism as a Marxist, Mei holds, removes its proletarian standpoint. Attacks on class struggle and the dictatorship of the proletariat are described as attacks on the Constitution and on the Marxist theory of law, which Mei says always serves a ruling group; the author cites US law on advocating the overthrow of government as comparison.

Mei proposes three responses. First, uphold Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought and the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, "and not some other ism". Second, study Xi Jinping's speeches as a weapon against Western ideological infiltration. Third, build a Chinese-style discourse system for sinified Marxism while criticising erroneous currents, following Xi's calls in 2013 and 2016. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-aligned Marxist theorist in 2016 classified and rebutted challenges to official Marxism, including attacks on foreign "Marxisms".
quoteEn: First, holding fast to the Communist Party of China's Marxist conception means upholding Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought and the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and not some other ism.
quoteZh: 第一，坚守中国共产党的马克思主义理念，就是要坚持马克思列宁主义、毛泽东思想、中国特色社会主义理论体系，而不是别的什么主义。

glossary.explanation: A label used in Party discourse for interpretations that question or negate the official account of Party and national history, including the revolutionary and socialist periods.

glossary.zh: 中国特色社会主义理论体系
glossary.pinyin: Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì lǐlùn tǐxì
glossary.en: the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: The official name for the body of Party theory from Deng Xiaoping Theory onwards, presented as the latest stage of the sinification of Marxism.

glossary.literal: the Party's basic line (one centre, two basic points)
glossary.explanation: The post-1978 formula of making economic development the central task while upholding the Four Cardinal Principles and reform and opening up.
The policy of economic reform and engagement with the outside world launched in 1978.
A Marxist concept for working-class state power in the transition to communism. Chinese texts equate it with the 'people's democratic dictatorship' in the Constitution.

t: Ideological work bears on the future and destiny of the Party and the state
zh: 意识形态工作关乎党和国家前途命运
paras: Writing in 2016, Lu Yan presents a commentary that reads Xi Jinping's speeches since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as a systematic strategy for ideological work. The central claim is that ideological work is "extremely important" and bears on the Party's and the state's future. Xi's remarks, the author says, set out the direction, principles and rules for handling ideology under new conditions.

The piece follows Xi's statements under five headings: giving ideological work extreme priority; maintaining ideological resolve; keeping the people at the centre; strengthening identification with socialist ideology; and strengthening the sense of responsibility for ideological work. It draws mainly on Xi's addresses to national propaganda and ideology conferences, the February 2016 symposium on Party media work, remarks during his European visit and talks with Peking University students. The author paraphrases and endorses these remarks, adding little independent analysis.

Lu argues first that economic construction remains the central task but cannot excuse neglect of ideology. The two must support each other, and the author holds that a regime's collapse often begins in the realm of ideas, so that leadership, management and discourse power over ideological work must never slip from the Party's hands. Second, ideological resolve is said to rest on faith in Marxism, confidence in the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics, cultural confidence, and a selective openness to foreign culture that avoids wholesale copying of Western methods. Third, the author insists that Party spirit and the people's character are unified: upholding one is upholding the other, and separating them is wrong in theory and harmful in practice.

On building identification, Lu proposes shared development outcomes, ideals-and-convictions education for Party members and wider society, and fostering the core socialist values. The final section calls for Party committees to bear primary responsibility, with secretaries as first persons responsible, and for a "big propaganda" approach involving the whole Party. This approach stresses positive messaging while not abandoning "struggle" in public opinion on matters of principle. Read the original if you want a compact digest of how Party commentators in 2016 summarised Xi Jinping's ideological-work doctrine and its institutional requirements.
quoteEn: Upholding the unity of Party spirit and the people's character means upholding political principle, keeping to the correct orientation, and uniting the expression of the Party's positions with the reflection of the people's voice.
quoteZh: 坚持党性和人民性相统一，就是要坚持讲政治，把握正确导向，把体现党的主张和反映人民心声统一起来。

glossary.explanation: The Party's work of shaping thought, public opinion, culture and propaganda, treated as a core responsibility of Party committees at every level.

glossary.en: Party spirit and the people's character
glossary.explanation: A pairing used in Party discourse for loyalty to the Party and service to the people; official texts hold that the two are identical in essence.
The ability to set the terms of public debate and shape how issues are framed.
Confidence in China's own cultural traditions and socialist culture, presented by Xi Jinping as underlying confidence in the path, theory and system.
A twelve-word official set of values: prosperity, democracy, civility, harmony; freedom, equality, justice, rule of law; patriotism, dedication, integrity, friendliness.
The idea that propaganda and ideology work is the task of the whole Party and government, not only of propaganda departments.

t: The four characteristics of the theoretical form of socialism with Chinese characteristics
zh: 中国特色社会主义理论形态的四大特征
source: Theory of Socialism with Chinese Characteristics (《中国特色社会主义理论》), 2016 no. 1
paras: Writing in 2016, Xin Xiangyang asks what kind of theoretical system the theory of socialism with Chinese characteristics is. Xin distinguishes academic systems built on concepts, judgements and inference (Locke, Kant, Hegel, Heidegger and others) from "practical" systems. These appear as resolutions, talks, notes and letters that look independent but are internally linked and answer a connected set of basic questions. Xin places the Chinese theoretical system in the second type and gives it four features: direct engagement with reality, collective wisdom, practical logic and diverse vehicles.

The article takes each feature in turn and traces it through the main components of the system: Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and the speeches of Xi Jinping. Xin draws on Party congress reports, plenum decisions and leaders' speeches. The examples include the basic economic system of the primary stage of socialism, ideas of development, the socialist core values and the five development concepts for the 13th Five-Year Plan period.

Xin argues that each body of theory arose from a concrete problem. Deng's theory answered what socialism is and how to build it after the Cultural Revolution. The Three Represents added how to build the Party, in the wake of the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union. The Scientific Outlook responded to questions of development, and Xi's speeches address problems such as the economic slowdown, social mobility and judicial fairness. Xin cites successive Party congress reports to show that each theory is described as the product of collective wisdom, and that every generation of leaders has answered the same basic question afresh. The practical logic is shown by the step-by-step growth of ideas such as the basic economic system, from the 1984 decision on economic reform through the 13th and 15th Party Congresses to Xi's formulation of the Two Unwaverings. Finally, Xin contends that after a proletarian party takes power, theoretical innovation appears less in large treatises than in congress reports, plenum decisions and leaders' speeches.

Xin concludes that these features make the system a living, practice-based body of theory that develops with practice. Xin treats the documents and speeches as the system's core theoretical achievements, including Deng's 1992 southern tour talks, Xi's eight criteria for judging a democratic political system and the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want a Party-theorist's account of why Chinese leaders' speeches and Party documents are treated as theory, with a detailed chronology of the sources.
quoteEn: This is a practice-oriented theoretical system. The theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics belongs to this type of system.
quoteZh: 这是一种实践型的理论体系。中国特色社会主义理论体系就属于这样一种体系。

glossary.explanation: A guiding ideology associated with Jiang Zemin, introduced around 2000. It holds that the Party represents advanced productive forces, the orientation of advanced culture and the fundamental interests of the overwhelming majority of the people.
Hu Jintao's guiding concept from the early 2000s. It stresses people-centred, comprehensive, coordinated and sustainable development.
The official characterisation of China's present stage of development, set out at the 13th Party Congress in 1987. It is used to justify a mixed economy and long-term reform.
The policy of unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector while unwaveringly encouraging, supporting and guiding the non-public sector.
A slogan put forward by Xi Jinping in 2012–13, centred on national rejuvenation and the well-being of the people.

t: Reflections on strengthening Party discipline under the new circumstances
zh: 新形势下加强党的纪律建设的思考
source: Studies on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics, 2016 no. 1
paras: Writing in 2016, Yuan Xiuli asks why Party discipline has been placed in a more prominent position since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and how discipline-building can be made standardised, institutionalised and routine. The article argues that strict discipline is a historical and practical necessity for a Marxist ruling party. It presents Xi Jinping's stress on observing discipline and respecting rules as an inheritance of the Party's traditions and a guarantee for the "Four-Pronged Comprehensive Strategy".

The article has three parts. The first gives four reasons why discipline must be strengthened: the nature of a Marxist party, the Party's own tradition, the demands of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and the requirements of governing the country according to law. The second sets out new formulations since 2012. The third turns to implementation, including the revised Code of Integrity and Self-Discipline and the Regulations on Disciplinary Actions issued in 2015.

In the first part, Yuan draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin and Deng Xiaoping, and on a line of Party leaders after Deng, to present discipline as a condition of unity and effectiveness. Yuan also describes challenges at home and abroad to the Party's legitimacy and leadership, and calls the question of whether the Party or the law is greater a "political trap" and a false proposition. The second part holds that Party rules are stricter than state law and that discipline comes before law, since law-breaking by members begins with breaking discipline. It stresses political discipline and political rules (the "five musts"), equality of all members before discipline, tightening the "cage" of institutions, and combining rule-based governance of the Party with moral self-cultivation.

Yuan concludes that obeying Party discipline is unconditional and that intra-Party regulations must not become "paper tigers". The article calls for a fuller regulatory system, stronger enforcement, and continued reform of discipline-inspection bodies, including nomination procedures for discipline officials and the inspection system. It also calls for discipline to become a "live high-voltage wire", with problems caught early and handled firmly. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how the Party justified its discipline campaign in 2015–16, including the ordering of discipline, rules and law.
quoteEn: When Party members break the law, it begins with breaking discipline.
quoteZh: 党员“破法”，始于“破纪”。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the Xi Jinping era, which stresses strict management of Party members, discipline and anti-corruption work. It is listed as one element of the "Four-Pronged Comprehensive Strategy".

Xi Jinping's strategic framework announced in 2014–15: building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, deepening reform, governing the country according to law, and strictly governing the Party.
A concept Xi Jinping stressed in 2015. It covers unwritten norms and working conventions of the Party that complement written discipline.

The body of rules issued by the Party for its own organisation and members, with the Party Constitution as its basis. Official discourse since 2012 has stressed building a system of them alongside state law.

glossary.zh: 中国共产党纪律处分条例
glossary.literal: Disciplinary Sanctions Regulations of the Communist Party of China
glossary.explanation: A Party regulation, revised in 2015, that lists violations in six categories (political, organisational, integrity, mass, work and lifestyle discipline) and the penalties for them.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: On the think-tank function of ideological and political education
zh: 论思想政治教育的智库功能
source: Studies on Ideological and Political Education, 2015 no. 5
paras: Writing in 2015, Li Liaoning asks how ideological and political education (sixiang zhengzhi jiaoyu) should understand and exercise a think-tank function. The starting point is the call of the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) to build new types of think tanks with Chinese characteristics, followed by the January 2015 General Office opinions on the subject, which include universities. Li argues that this function is not part of the field's traditional educational role but an extension of it, and that the field should consciously act as an adviser to the ruling party.

The article has three parts. The first places the think-tank function within existing research, which has dealt mainly with social and individual functions, and compares ideological and political education with ordinary think tanks. The second sets out the field's advantages and its shortcomings. The third proposes four measures: reforming research evaluation, cultivating talent, building information resources, and expanding outside exchange.

Li defines the think-tank function as the role played in strategic research, policy advice, theoretical innovation, guiding public opinion, social service and external communication. Unlike the educational function, which publicises policies already made, it moves earlier, to research on ideological questions before policy is set. Li holds that the field resembles other think tanks in doing non-profit policy research with relative independence, but cannot be 'neutral' because its strongly ideological character requires it to serve the ruling party and reflect the interests of the broad population. The listed advantages are high official attention to ideology, a large body of researchers, and growing state funding. The listed weaknesses are a shortage of outstanding research (the author cites few top prizes for the Marxism discipline), weak 'participation' and 'evaluation' awareness among practitioners who equate being the Party's mouthpiece with not thinking independently, and an evaluation system that does not count policy reports.

Li's proposals include crediting policy reports, blue books and advisory memoranda in evaluation and promotion, and organising talent in four circles from outstanding to peripheral. They also include a 'revolving door' between universities, government and enterprises, big-data resource building, and closer ties with government, other think tanks and the media. Li says influence on government decisions is what finally decides whether the function works. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar in 2015 justified and organised an advisory role for ideological and political education within the new think-tank policy.
quoteEn: The proposal of the think-tank function is a role-awareness on the part of ideological and political education.
quoteZh: 智库功能的提出，是思想政治教育的角色自觉。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese discipline and practice of shaping the political views, ideology and moral character of citizens, especially students, in line with the ruling party's aims. It is a second-level discipline under Marxist theory.

glossary.en: new types of think tanks with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: A policy goal set out at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) and in the 2015 opinions, aimed at building advisory research bodies that serve Party and government decision-making.
Used in official Chinese discourse for the guiding system of ideas of the state, with Marxism as the leading ideology. Ideological work is treated as a key task of the Party.

t: Correctly grasping the characteristics of our era and upholding and developing the socialist cause
zh: 正确把握时代特征与坚持和发展社会主义事业
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2016 no. 2
paras: Writing in 2016, the author asks how Marxists should define the present era and why this matters for upholding socialism. The article's thesis is that the era is the long epoch, opened by the October Revolution, in which socialism gradually replaces capitalism. Within it, the author says, there are shorter stages, and both levels must be held together. Losing sight of either one, the article warns, leads to dogmatism or to disorientation.

The article has three parts. The first draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Sartre and Deng Xiaoping to define an "era" by its mode of production and class relations, and to answer claims that Marxism is outdated and socialism has failed after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The second discusses the stages of the era, from Mao Zedong's "war and revolution" to Deng's "peace and development", and Mao's views on war and peace. The third turns to Deng's warning of "two cold wars" and sets out four practical tasks for China.

The author argues that the end of the Cold War did not end the confrontation between two social systems, and that imperialism's contradiction with socialism and with oppressed peoples remains the basic contradiction of the age. Citing Brzezinski's later writings, the author claims that Western triumphalism has faded. Treating "peace and development" as the name of the whole era is, in this reading, a mistake that contradicts Deng and plays down imperialism and hegemony. Following Lenin on the "bloodless front", the author describes "peaceful evolution" and "colour revolutions" as Western tools against socialist states and the Third World, and counts the 1989 protests and the 2014 "Occupy Central" movement as cases or near-cases.

From this, the author proposes four tasks. China should keep its theoretical resolve in foreign policy and not abandon Marxist class analysis. It must avoid "subversive mistakes" in reform and opening up, notably departing from public ownership's leading role and common prosperity. It must resist neoliberalism, historical nihilism, democratic socialism, constitutional democracy, universal values and similar currents. It must also tackle the loss of ideals and convictions among Party members, in line with the Party's strict self-governance and Xi Jinping's 2013 warning. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-theory journal in 2016 linked Marxist era theory to ideological security and "colour revolution" concerns.
quoteEn: The era of which we speak includes both the large historical epoch and its different stages, the dialectical unity of the two; this is the Marxist view of the era that we must uphold.
quoteZh: 我们所说的时代，是包括大的历史发展时代以及不同的发展阶段，是二者的辩证统一，这是我们必须坚持的马克思主义的时代观。

glossary.explanation: A term for the popular protest movements that toppled governments in Georgia, Ukraine, Kyrgyzstan and elsewhere. Chinese official and academic writing often presents them as externally backed attempts at regime change.
A Chinese Communist Party term for the alleged Western strategy of undermining socialist states through ideological and cultural influence rather than force.
In Party usage, a label for views that are said to deny or distort the Party's and socialism's history. It is commonly listed among 'erroneous trends of thought'.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in China from 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.
A socialist goal of shared wealth for all, repeatedly invoked by Deng Xiaoping and later leaders as opposed to polarisation between rich and poor.

t: Warnings from the Soviet collapse for building a Marxist ruling party
zh: 苏联解体对马克思主义执政党建设的警示
paras: More than twenty years after the Soviet collapse, Xue Yan asks what it teaches about building a Marxist ruling party. Writing in 2016 in a commentary for Red Flag Manuscripts, the author acknowledges that the collapse had many causes, including nationality problems, loss of belief, reform and the federal state form. Xue nonetheless argues that the problems and defects of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) in its work as a ruling party were what finally brought the Union down.

The article is organised around six lessons, each followed by a short comparison with the Communist Party of China (CPC). They cover guiding ideology, the regular replacement of leaders, clean government and privileged strata, the capacity to face and correct mistakes, control over reform, and the handling of international relations, especially Western "peaceful evolution". Evidence comes from CPSU party statutes, the careers of Soviet leaders from Khrushchev to Gorbachev, and statements by Nikolai Ryzhkov, Boris Kuzmin-style insiders and others, along with Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping.

Xue's central claim is that the CPSU drifted away from Marxism-Leninism until, under Gorbachev, it recast itself as a party of "all-human values" and "humane, democratic socialism". In Xue's account, the lack of a lawful system for replacing leaders let unqualified figures reach the top, and a privileged stratum enriched itself and lost popular support. The author adds that weak self-correction, the wholesale denunciation of Stalin and reform driven by personal preference or the wrong direction left the party unable to steer. The author also holds that the West used ideological infiltration and cultivated agents to bring about peaceful evolution, citing Margaret Thatcher's remark that the West promoted Gorbachev.

Xue concludes that socialist countries must reform in ways that keep the country from "changing colour", and that communist parties must be built so as to keep their vanguard character. For the CPC, this means upholding Marxism as guiding thought, selecting reliable successors, maintaining clean government, admitting and correcting errors, keeping reform on course and guarding against peaceful evolution. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese Party commentary in 2016 drew lessons from the Soviet collapse for Party building.
quoteEn: The vitality of socialism lies in reform, but if reform departs from the correct direction, it too can destroy socialism.
quoteZh: 社会主义的生命力在改革，但改革偏离正确方向，也会断送社会主义。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese Party discourse for the alleged Western strategy of undermining socialist states through ideological, cultural and economic influence rather than force. It originated in Cold War-era discussions and is used by the author in this sense.
The claim that the Communist Party leads society as its most advanced force and must keep its purity. The term is used in Party-building discourse.

t: Upholding the Four Cardinal Principles and opposing bourgeois liberalization as the Party's most fundamental political discipline
zh: 坚持四项基本原则、反对资产阶级自由化是党的一项最根本的政治纪律
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2016, Tian Gaiwei comments on Article 45 of the revised Disciplinary Regulations of the Communist Party of China, in force from 1 January 2016. That article prescribes expulsion from the Party for publicly voicing bourgeois-liberal positions, opposing the Four Cardinal Principles or opposing the Party's reform and opening-up decisions. Tian argues that upholding the Four Cardinal Principles and opposing bourgeois liberalization form the Party's most fundamental political discipline and its greatest political rule.

The piece has two parts. The first traces how the discipline arose and was codified: Deng Xiaoping's 1979 speech, the 1987 Central Committee notice, the 1992 insertion into the Party Constitution, the 2003 regulations, and the 2016 revision. The second sets out how the Party has defined bourgeois liberalization, citing Hu Qiaomu in 1981, Deng in 1986 and the 1987 notice, and why the struggle is long-term. Throughout, Tian leans on statements by Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping.

Tian defines bourgeois liberalization as a current of thought directly opposed to the Four Cardinal Principles, whose core is denying the Party's leadership and the socialist system. Its forms change, the author says, but its opposition to those principles does not, and this serves as the test for identifying it. In Tian's account, it has recently appeared as promotion of Western "universal values" and "constitutionalism", multiparty and separation-of-powers systems, and slander of the Party by some members, including online influencers. The 2016 regulations therefore extend penalties to those who supply channels and platforms for such views. Tian cites Deng's view that the struggle would last decades, and argues that the influence of liberalization can be removed at root only when socialist modernization has clearly shown its advantages over capitalism.

Tian concludes that, as the Party nears the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, it needs iron discipline, and that bourgeois liberalization is the gravest erosion of it. Quoting Xi Jinping that strict discipline begins with political discipline, Tian calls on members to bind themselves by Article 45 and to struggle openly against violations. Read the original if you want to see how a 2016 Party-journal commentary links the new disciplinary regulations to Deng-era formulations on liberalization.
quoteEn: Opposing bourgeois liberalization is a long-term task.
quoteZh: 反对资产阶级自由化是一项长期的任务。

glossary.explanation: Formulated by Deng Xiaoping in 1979: keeping to the socialist road, the people's democratic dictatorship, the leadership of the Communist Party, and Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought. They are written into the Party Constitution.

A term used in Party discourse since the early 1980s for ideas seen as promoting Western-style liberal politics and capitalism and as challenging Party leadership. It is applied by the Party to a range of political and intellectual trends.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central goal of Party leaders, especially under Xi Jinping, of restoring China's national strength and international standing by the mid-twenty-first century.

t: The European refugee crisis and the predicament of "universal values"
zh: 欧洲难民危机与“普世价值”的困境
paras: Writing in early 2016, Zhang Weiwei takes up the refugee flows into Europe since 2015 and argues that they are directly linked to the "universal values" the West promoted in the Middle East. In Zhang's account, the crisis exposes paradoxes and dilemmas in the idea of "universal values" itself. Zhang suggests that reflecting on this matters for China's development and the world's future.

The commentary has three sections. The first describes what Zhang calls the arrogance of the "universal values" camp and its cost. The second sets out four paradoxes revealed by the crisis. The third draws lessons for China and for global governance. Zhang's evidence is the two waves of Middle Eastern "democratization", the Iraq War and the "Greater Middle East" plan from 2003, then the "Arab Spring" from around 2011. Zhang also points to the Syrian, Libyan, Egyptian, Tunisian and Yemeni outcomes and to European disputes over refugee quotas.

Zhang traces the West's missionary zeal to a view of history in which the Western model is the final stage, together with a Christian missionary tradition. Zhang says Western powers never asked ordinary people in the region what they wanted. On this account, the result was state collapse, extremism and refugees. The four paradoxes are as follows. First, these values were detached from local national conditions and could not solve sectarian, ethnic, demographic or economic problems. Second, Western electoral politics, in which politicians answer only to their own voters, runs against the principle of universal human rights, as in the fences, quota disputes and Angela Merkel's falling support. Third, the values cannot accommodate multiculturalism, as rising xenophobia and the right show. Fourth, abstract values give way to concrete national interests, including those of Britain, France and the United States.

Zhang concludes that Chinese readers should always ask "why" of values that claim to be universal, to avoid being misled by Western discourse. Zhang says the crisis underlines the significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Zhang predicts the decline of Western discursive hegemony and calls on China to offer its own ideas, such as "peace and development", as a basis for global governance. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2016 Qiushi article used the refugee crisis to criticise "universal values" and promote a Chinese alternative discourse.
quoteEn: Of abstract values that claim to be universal and free of limits of time and space, we must always ask "why".
quoteZh: 对自称是普世的、不受时间和空间限制的抽象的价值观念，我们一定要问一个为什么。

glossary.explanation: The idea that values such as freedom, democracy and human rights apply to all societies. Chinese official and Party-theory writing often criticises it as a vehicle for Western ideology.
The official name for China's political and economic path since reform and opening up. It is presented as Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions.
A term in Chinese commentary for the dominance of Western concepts and narratives in international debate. Authors use it to argue for developing China's own discourse.
The wave of protests and uprisings that began in Tunisia in 2010–11 and spread across the Arab world. Zhang puts the term in scare quotes and contrasts it with an "Arab Winter".

t: Guiding online public opinion within ideological work in universities
zh: 试论高校意识形态工作视域下的网络舆情引导
source: Journal of Huaiyin Normal University (Philosophy and Social Sciences), 2016 no. 1
paras: Writing in 2016, Zheng Jie and Chen Yizhang ask how Chinese universities should guide online public opinion as part of their ideological work. They argue that universities are an important front in ideological struggle and that, with the spread of mobile internet, students have become major producers, spreaders and recipients of online opinion, and are in the authors' view especially easy to mislead. Guiding that opinion is therefore a necessary part of strengthening ideological work on campus.

The article opens with survey figures from the China Internet Network Information Center on student internet use, and cites the January 2015 central guideline on strengthening propaganda and ideological work in universities. It then describes how universities currently handle online opinion, lists five shortcomings, and sets out a five-part countermeasure system. The authors rely on policy documents, survey statistics and a few Chinese studies of campus opinion management rather than on case studies.

On current practice, the authors report that most universities run student-staffed monitoring teams under teacher supervision, sort opinion into ordinary, social and campus categories, and keep basic emergency-response procedures. They identify five problems: opinion education is one-sided and consists of demands without explanation; information management is passive because platforms such as Baidu Tieba are run by companies or student moderators who may decline to cooperate; monitoring depends on manual labour and covers only a sliver of online content; guidance is crude, relying on warnings and deleted posts that may provoke resistance; and universities react after outbreaks rather than shaping the environment beforehand.

In response they propose a 'five-in-one' prevention and control mechanism with five layers. These are ideological education that builds students' own 'immunity'; early warning based on big data and mathematical models; better search technology, combining web crawlers and keyword filtering with manual collection on private platforms; more varied guidance through student-style online comments, student opinion leaders and authoritative releases; and a stronger organisational structure with full- and part-time staff led by the propaganda department or network management centre. The authors conclude that universities must adopt these measures to protect students from harmful information and keep ideological work secure. Read the original if you want a concise 2016 account of how Chinese universities describe and plan to manage campus internet opinion.
quoteEn: Only if universities actively meet these changes, think proactively, innovate technically and improve opinion work, guarding online public opinion as the most important gateway of campus ideological construction, can students' thinking be better protected from chaotic information.
quoteZh: 高校只有主动迎接这些变化、积极思考、创新技术手段、优化舆情工作，把好高校意识形态建设中网络舆情这一最主要的关卡，才能更好地使大学生的思想不受杂乱信息的侵害

glossary.explanation: The Party-state's work of managing and promoting official ideology in education, media and culture, with Marxism as the guiding doctrine. It is stressed as a priority since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
The collective views, emotions and demands that internet users express on public affairs and hot issues. Chinese institutions monitor and guide it as a matter of social and ideological management.
The Party's system of propaganda, ideological education and cultural management. In Chinese usage 'propaganda' (xuānchuán) is a neutral term for official communication.

Here a mechanism of five integrated layers: education, early warning, monitoring, handling and organisational support. The same phrase also names the Party's five-sphere overall plan for national development.

t: Accurately grasping the new situation in the contest for ideological discourse power on the internet
zh: 准确把握互联网意识形态话语权争夺的新形势
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2015, Li Jiangjing and Xu Hongye ask how Marxism can keep its guiding position in China's ideological sphere as information technology changes the contest for discourse power online. They argue that this contest has taken on new features and that Party and state must understand them in order to respond. Their answer is that mainstream ideology has to win in three areas: who can spread a message, who sets the agenda, and who controls the carriers of discourse.

The article has three parts. It first identifies three key nodes in the formation of internet ideological discourse power: the right of discourse subjects to disseminate, the right to set topics, and the right to use discourse carriers. It then describes three new features of the contest. It ends with proposals centred on theoretical innovation, control of capital and technology, and three practical paths. Examples include the 2015 debate over Western values in universities, the 2013 "Prism" affair, and the May 2015 Qing'an shooting incident.

The authors hold that ordinary users have equal rights of expression, but the large media outlets that hold network resources still dominate dissemination. They treat agenda-setting as the hinge of the process, because whoever frames an event shapes what people think and how. They see control of carriers as the most basic node. In their account, the United States dominates the root servers, the ICANN domain-name system and the markets of firms such as Microsoft and Intel. They say the contest has moved from holding platforms to seizing topics, from spontaneous to self-conscious opinion, and from complete narratives to fragmented dissemination. As examples they cite misleading headlines, attacks on revolutionary heroes, and "historical nihilism".

Li and Xu call for spreading innovative theory that combines Marxism with China's realities, and for gaining a say over internet firms where capital is concentrated. They also call for China to develop its own core technologies. On the practical side, they propose renewing the form of discourse while keeping its Marxist core, and having mainstream media set agendas first, helped by opinion leaders and online propagandists. They also propose combining united-front work with struggle: engaging users' concerns while debating and rebutting dissenters and hostile forces. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese ideological-work scholarship framed online opinion contests in 2015, and how it justified state and Party strategies for them.
quoteEn: Holding the right to set topics online lets one influence opinion by supplying information and arranging meaning, steering what people think about and how they think, and this is the hinge in realising internet ideological discourse power.
quoteZh: 拥有网络话语主题设置权，可以通过提供信息和安排意义来影响舆论，左右人们“想什么”、“怎样想”，是互联网意识形态话语权实现的枢纽环节。

glossary.explanation: The capacity to shape public understanding, values and opinion through what is said and how it is framed. In Chinese Party scholarship it is closely tied to preserving Marxism's leading position.
A label used in Party discourse for views that are said to deny or distort the history of the Chinese revolution and socialism, including the reputations of its leaders and heroes.
A concept from communication studies, referring to the power to decide which topics and framings dominate public attention. The article treats it as the hinge of discourse power.
A Party approach of winning over and uniting different groups. The authors pair it with struggle (dòuzhēng) in dealing with different opponents online.

t: The values crisis of the American Dream
zh: 美国梦的价值观危机
source: Journal of Jiangsu University (Social Science Edition), 2015 no. 6
paras: Zeng Zhihao asks what values the American Dream carries and why, in the author's reading, those values have fallen into crisis. The article argues that the Dream is not always benign: it can become a nightmare or an illusion, and some of the problems it has produced are chronic ones that its champions could not resolve. Zeng traces them mainly to its excessive materialism and individualism. The piece, first published in 2015 in the Journal of Jiangsu University (Social Sciences Edition), is a short essay rather than an empirical study.

The article moves through the Dream's main value components in turn: materialism and the worship of wealth, individualism, and a culture of self-indulgence. For each, it lists social consequences, including poverty and homelessness, loneliness and mental illness, drug use and gambling, and crime. It then turns to a counter-tradition of democracy, equality, tolerance and community responsibility, which Zeng describes as having balanced the Dream for much of American history. Zeng draws on John Dewey's critique of consumerism and on episodes such as the Depression-era New Deal and the 1960s counterculture.

Zeng argues that unrestrained pursuit of money has produced an extreme wealth gap, with tens of millions living below the poverty line, and that individualism has degenerated into laissez-faire selfishness in a society built on competition rather than cooperation. Drawing on Dewey, Zeng contends that consumption and enjoyment are not values in themselves; they become values only when subjected to intelligent judgment and reflection. Crime statistics from the late twentieth century and the rise of hippies and drug use are offered as evidence of a disillusionment that the author links to the Dream's collapse. Zeng also adds an ecological dimension, saying that unlimited materialism is incompatible with the earth's ecology and with global warming.

Zeng concludes that the United States must recover a moral and communitarian dream, such as the small-town ideal and the collective spirit of the 1930s, to curb materialist fervour and renew civil society. The author states that the country's ugly and corrupt side is determined by the capitalist system itself, and that it can only advance amid a mix of problems and hopes. The essay ends by asking whether new dreams will arise to shape America's future. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese academic essay in ideological education presents American values and their perceived failings.
quoteEn: Individualism itself contains the seeds of extremism; as the capitalist system developed and matured, individualism gradually turned into laissez-faire and selfishness.
quoteZh: 个人主义本身内含了走向极端化的诱因，随着资本主义制度的发展和完善，个人主义逐渐演变为自由放任和自私自利

t: A comparison of Marx's and Aristotle's views of happiness
zh: 马克思和亚里士多德幸福观比较
paras: Chen Wanqiu asks what genuine happiness is, where a theory of happiness should begin and how people reach it. The article argues that Marx and Aristotle, despite their differences, both treat happiness as grounded in human nature, as multi-layered, and as realised through practice rather than fantasy.

The article compares the two thinkers under three headings: human nature as the logical starting point, the rich content of happiness, and practice as the route to happiness. It draws on Aristotle's ethics and politics, and on Marx's Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Capital, the introduction to the critique of Hegel's philosophy of right and his criticism of Epicurus. A final section draws lessons for present-day China.

Chen argues that both thinkers see human beings as unities of natural and social attributes. Aristotle, with his claim that the human being is a political animal, first glimpsed this; Marx, in Chen's reading, states it more accurately by locating the human essence in sociality. Both reject a one-sided view that reduces happiness to ascetic denial or to sensual pleasure. Aristotle ranks bodily, political and contemplative lives and names contemplation the highest happiness, whereas Marx treats happiness as a unity of material and spiritual life. For Marx the highest good is the free and all-round development of individual talents and creativity. On the route to happiness, Aristotle calls it the fruit of rational activity over a whole lifetime but ends by privileging contemplation, which Chen calls one-sided. Marx replaces contemplation with practice, above all labour, and makes the liberation of labour the precondition of happiness.

Chen draws three lessons. Happiness must be understood through human duality, so individual and social happiness are interdependent, with social happiness as the foundation and the higher of the two. Spiritual happiness must be taken seriously against materialism, consumerism and hedonism, and Chen mentions the 'house slave' and 'car slave' phenomena. Illusions must be abandoned in favour of creative practice, with the state's comprehensive deepening of reform and law-based governance cited as creating conditions for the people's happiness. Read the original if you want a concise comparative account of Marxist and Aristotelian eudaimonism, linked to Chinese debates on contemporary well-being.
quoteEn: Happiness arises from practice, and practice gives birth to happiness.
quoteZh: 幸福产生于实践，实践催生幸福。

t: Experience of building a rule-of-law culture in Singapore
zh: 新加坡法治文化建设的经验
source: China Party and Government Cadres Forum (Zhongguo dangzheng ganbu luntan), 2015 no. 12
paras: This short commentary asks why Singapore, a small resource-poor state, became a modern, orderly and clean-governed country within about thirty years. Jiao Yuli takes up Lee Kuan Yew's remark that the key to Singapore's success is the rule of law, and argues that Singapore's distinctive rule-of-law culture is worth close study and emulation. The piece was first published in 2015 under a slightly longer title that included the word 'lessons'.

Jiao defines rule-of-law culture as the values-centred patterns of thought and behaviour towards legal life that a society builds up over time, and as the cultural basis without which the rule of law cannot work. The article then sets out three features of the Singapore case: a comprehensive legal system, a 'shared values' framework, and a popular faith in law backed by strict enforcement.

On the first, Jiao says Singapore has over 400 statutes regulating matters from political institutions to parking and chewing-gum sales, including a set of anti-corruption laws.
