On the second, the 1991 White Paper on Shared Values is said to guide legal culture, and housing legislation supporting the 'home ownership' policy is offered as an example. On the third, Jiao argues that equal application of law explains public support for harsh penalties such as caning, citing a 1994 Straits Times poll in which nearly 90 per cent favoured keeping it. Cases of ministers punished for corruption, and Lee Kuan Yew's request for an investigation of his own property purchase, are presented as proof of equality before the law.

Jiao concludes that Singapore's experience, in which complete legislation, shared values and impartial enforcement reinforce one another, merits study. The text offers no explicit policy proposals beyond this call for learning from the case. Read the original if you want a brief, favourable Chinese Party-journal account of how Singapore's legal culture is presented to cadres as a model.
quoteEn: Equality before the law has become the essence of Singapore's rule-of-law culture, because such law is beneficial to Singapore and worthy of trust.
quoteZh: 法律面前人人平等已成为新加坡法治文化的精髓，因为这样的法律对新加坡是有益的，是值得信任的。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese legal and political writing referring to the values, beliefs and habits through which a society accepts and practises the rule of law. It is treated as the cultural basis of legal institutions.
Singapore's official set of five values, set out in a 1991 White Paper, which stress community over the individual, consensus, racial and religious harmony, and the family as the basis of society.

t: Making the "Three Stricts and Three Reals" a routine practice
zh: 推进“三严三实”常态化
paras: This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in October 2015, asks how the campaign of "Three Stricts and Three Reals" (sanyan sanshi) can become a lasting practice rather than a one-off drive. Yu Xiangdong argues that the special education programme is a routine task of the Party for eliminating unhealthy tendencies, and that it should be made routine in three areas: ideological education, observance of rules and discipline, and supervision and inspection.

The piece begins with Xi Jinping's call on Party members and cadres, especially leaders, to keep the principles in mind and apply a spirit of strictness and realism. It cites the General Office's plan for county- and department-level leading cadres, which presents the programme as an extension of the Party's mass line education campaign. That plan, Yu notes, requires no batches, stages or phases. The commentary then takes the three areas in turn.

On ideological education, Yu holds that correct understanding is the key to implementation. Cadres are to treat study as a habit, study the 18th Party Congress (2012) and Xi Jinping's speeches, and draw lessons from positive and negative examples. On rules and discipline, Yu calls for firm awareness of the Party constitution, the law and the masses, so that the principles become part of daily conduct. On supervision, Yu cites Lenin on monitoring and punishing non-execution of decrees, and proposes improving three mechanisms: organisational, mass and public-opinion supervision.

Yu concludes that study and propaganda alone are insufficient, and that routine education, discipline and all-round supervision are needed to make work-style improvement regular and lasting. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party press in 2015 framed the institutionalisation of the "Three Stricts and Three Reals" within full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.
quoteEn: Without rules there can be no order, and without practice everything is empty talk.
quoteZh: 无规矩不成方圆，无践行必为空谈。

glossary.explanation: A slogan introduced by Xi Jinping in 2014 asking officials to be strict in self-cultivation, in using power and in self-discipline, and to be honest in decisions, in starting undertakings and in conduct. A special education campaign for leading cadres was launched in 2015.

glossary.zh: 党的群众路线教育实践活动
glossary.pinyin: dǎng de qúnzhòng lùxiàn jiàoyù shíjiàn huódòng
glossary.literal: Party's mass line education and practice activity
glossary.explanation: A Party-wide rectification campaign of 2013–2014 aimed at combating formalism, bureaucracy, hedonism and extravagance among officials.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: An official formulation for strengthening Party discipline, work style and anti-corruption efforts, forming part of the Four-pronged Comprehensive Strategy from 2014–2015.

t: Full coverage, high standards, strict requirements
st: Studying the Code of Integrity and Self-Discipline and the Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of the Communist Party of China
zh: 全覆盖、高标准、严要求
zhSub: 学习《中国共产党廉洁自律准则》和《中国共产党纪律处分条例》
paras: Writing in early 2016, Yuan Xiuli introduces the newly revised Code of Integrity and Self-Discipline and the Regulations on Disciplinary Actions of the Communist Party of China, and argues that all Party members should study them closely. The author notes that, alongside wide approval, a few people have misread or attacked the documents, above all the ban on members "groundlessly criticising" major central Party policies, which some call a gag on free speech. Yuan treats such views as reflecting an incomplete grasp of Party discipline, and in a few cases deliberate distortion.

The commentary has two parts. The first sets out six features of the revised texts: major changes, broad scope, new content, strict requirements, high standards and practicability. The second explains why implementing them matters, under four headings: establishing the authority of Party rules, improving the Party's rule system, protecting centralised unity, and giving intra-Party and public supervision a basis in rules.

Yuan's central move is to present the Code as a positive list that cultivates virtue and the Regulations as a negative list that draws bottom lines, forming a "two-wheel drive" for governing the Party. The Code shrinks from 3,600-plus characters to about 280 and now covers all members, with higher demands on leading cadres. The Regulations reorganise offences into six categories of discipline, separate Party discipline from state law, and set standards stricter than the law. On the contested clause, Yuan distinguishes constructive criticism from destructive "groundless criticism". Members, the author says, may raise dissent through proper channels, enter reservations while carrying out decisions, and appeal to higher bodies. Public opposition to central decisions is barred, and Yuan sees nothing to fear for intra-Party democracy, since democratic centralism requires unity of action.

Yuan concludes that the two documents turn the achievements of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) into regular institutions, and signal that discipline will only tighten. The author adds that supervision and accountability must be strengthened together, and that every cadre must absorb the documents' spirit and put them into practice. Read the original if you want an official-line defence of the 2015 Party discipline revisions, especially the case made for the ban on "groundless criticism" of central policy.
quoteEn: Criticism is constructive, whereas groundless criticism is destructive and even ill-intentioned.
quoteZh: 批评是建设性的，而妄议是破坏性的，甚至是别有用心的。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping's leadership since 2012, covering anti-corruption, discipline and Party-building. It is one of the "Four Comprehensives".
The Party's organisational principle, combining intra-Party discussion with binding unity of action once decisions are taken.

t: Analysis of the state of online thought in 2015
zh: 2015年度网络思想状况分析
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (January 2016), Li Yanyan reviews the state of online thought and opinion in China during 2015 and looks ahead. The author argues that the year was complex and contentious, with new features in content, dissemination and influence, and that online ideological and cultural work needs strengthening.
The piece has two parts. The first sets out three notable features of 2015; the second offers recommendations for 2016, organised under ideological work, institutions and mechanisms, and personnel.

On the features, Li says the authorities showed stronger ability to set agendas and to govern the internet by law. Li cites the 70th anniversary of the victory in the War of Resistance, the second World Internet Conference, the draft Cybersecurity Law and a draft law on overseas NGOs. Online disputes also educated netizens, though cases such as the Langya Mountain debate and an attack on a patriotic young netizen discouraged some speakers. Fast-moving, interlinked media weakened the guiding power of traditional Party media, ideological topics drew sustained attention, and disputes involving police and military grew. For 2016, Li calls for awakening netizens' sense of ownership and judgement, and for training in historical and dialectical materialist thinking, so that the "silent majority" is not swayed by opinion leaders.

Li also proposes top-level design of online content production, dissemination and evaluation, including reform of academic evaluation, support for positive online opinion leaders and effect-oriented assessment. A propaganda force of Party cadres, volunteers and scholars should carry the online spread of core socialist values. Read the original if you want a concise official-academic view of how Chinese ideological work approached online opinion at the end of 2015.
quoteEn: The main force for spreading core socialist values online cannot and should not be spontaneous netizens.
quoteZh: 社会主义核心价值观网络传播的主力不能也不该是自发的网民。

glossary.explanation: A twelve-word set of values (such as prosperity, democracy, harmony, patriotism) promoted by the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as the basis of public ideology.
Influential online figures whose posts shape public discussion; the author treats them as able to dominate opinion.
Netizens who read online content but rarely post; the author sees them as the key group to be mobilised.

t: An important compass for promoting China's fine traditional culture
st: A reading of Xi Jinping's speech to the International Confucian Association
zh: 弘扬中国优秀传统文化的重要指导南针
paras: This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in September 2015, studies Xi Jinping's speech at the Fifth Member Congress of the International Confucian Association. Teng Wensheng argues that the speech is a major, far-sighted statement. He calls it both a compass for promoting China's fine traditional culture and a declaration on how different civilizations should learn from one another.

Teng first sets out eight points that he says the speech clarifies. They concern peace and development as the background of the era, the historical role of Confucianism and traditional culture, their characteristics and the values they contain, and the proper approach to other civilizations. They also cover the need to sift traditional culture, the study of tradition as a route to understanding Chinese national character, and the Communist Party's stance toward tradition. He then draws lessons for inheriting tradition and for exchange between civilizations.

On tradition, Teng argues that every present-day culture grows from a traditional base, so inheritance must be selective: take the essence, discard the dross, and pursue creative transformation and innovative development rather than copying. He rejects historical nihilism. He holds that Marxism's guiding role in China forms a unity of "one dominant strand, many strands" with traditional and progressive thought, and cites Confucianism's long dominance in feudal China, which did not stop other schools from functioning. On civilizations, he stresses that each is a nation's soul, that all are equal with no higher or lower, and that cultural hegemony is a road to decline.

Teng concludes that the International Confucian Association will follow the speech's principles, link the promotion of tradition with dialogue among civilizations, and tell the story of China's cultural continuity. He presents this as a contribution to world peace and to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want an officially aligned reading of Xi's 2014 Confucian speech and of how Party writers reconcile Marxism with traditional culture.
quoteEn: Every kind of traditional thought and culture carries certain historical limitations and is not all essence, so one must take its essence and discard its dross.
quoteZh: 任何一种传统思想文化都会带有某些历史的局限性，不会都是精华，因此对它们要取其精华、去其糟粕。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping from around 2012–13, stressing cooperation, win-win outcomes and shared interests among countries.

glossary.zh: 创造性转化、创新性发展
glossary.explanation: An official formula for dealing with traditional culture: adapting its forms and content to present needs rather than copying them.
A formula in which Marxism holds the guiding position in ideology while other thought currents coexist beneath it.
A term in Party discourse for views seen as denying or distorting the official historical record, including the value of China's past.

t: Strengthening the construction of a Marxist discourse system among contemporary youth
zh: 在当代青年中强化马克思主义话语体系建设
paras: Tan Jinsong and Huang Fanwen, writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2015, no. 20), take up the observation that part of China's young generation, raised in the reform era, is increasingly unfamiliar with or even hostile to the Marxist discourse system. The authors argue that strengthening this discourse among young people is an urgent task, because its absence threatens the continuity of socialism in China.

The article is organised in four parts: the main manifestations of the gap, its consequences, its causes, and proposed countermeasures. It is a short argumentative piece in the style of ideological and political education commentary, drawing on no case studies or data and relying on assertion and historical analogy, notably to the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.

The authors identify three manifestations: young people do not know Marxist vocabulary, their grounding in the classics and basic principles is weak, and their belief in Marxism is not firm. They say this matters because it hinders training successors for socialism, the transmission of Marxism, and resistance to what they call Western ideological infiltration and 'peaceful evolution', which they describe as now aimed at China's youth. They trace the problem to three causes: poorly delivered theoretical education that is cut off from students' interests; Western culture and values spread through media and consumption; and, at the deepest level, the value pluralism that accompanies a mix of ownership forms. In their reading, the economic base determines ideology, so individual-centred values growing with the non-public sector have marginalised Marxist discourse among some youth.

Tan and Huang propose three measures: make Marxist theory courses compulsory and improve their teaching so students accept them 'in ear, brain and heart'; strengthen young people's resistance to Western ideas, including strict screening of Western cultural products online and blocking material seen as maliciously discrediting socialism; and implement the dominant position of public ownership as the economic foundation of socialist ideology, while supporting the non-public sector but never allowing privatisation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-journal writing in 2015 framed youth ideology, Western cultural influence and public ownership as linked problems.
quoteEn: Whether Marxist discourse can be established among contemporary youth will affect the success or failure of the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics; this is by no means an exaggeration.
quoteZh: 马克思主义话语在当代青年中能否确立,将会影响到中国特色社会主义事业发展的成败,这绝非夸大其辞。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese Party discourse for the supposed Western strategy of undermining socialist states through cultural, ideological and economic influence rather than force.
The body of concepts, terms and modes of expression through which a theory or ideology is articulated and communicated.
The principle in China's basic economic system that public ownership remains the mainstay while multiple ownership forms develop alongside it.

t: Characteristics of US values export after the Cold War
st: Excerpt from "Characteristics of US values export after the Cold War and ideological education in China's universities"
zh: 冷战后美国价值观输出的特点
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2015 no. 9
paras: This short piece, published in a 2015 issue of a journal on ideological and political education, asks how the United States has exported its values since the Cold War ended. Liu argues that every US administration since then has given "values export" a very important place in its foreign strategy, and that the practice shows three features: moral deceptiveness, concealed forms and varied means.

Liu surveys the post-Cold War presidencies in turn: George H. W. Bush's "promotion and consolidation of democracy", the Clinton administration's three pillars of economy, security and democracy, George W. Bush's "Greater Middle East" democratic remodelling plan, and the Obama administration's "smart power" diplomacy. The three features are then illustrated with cases from China, Iraq, Central Asia and the Middle East.

On moral deceptiveness, Liu contends that the US uses its media strength and discursive hegemony to promote separation of powers and party systems as "universal values", to demonise socialist states, and to dress interventionism in moral language such as "human rights above sovereignty". On concealment, Liu says Washington often works through NGOs, media, think tanks, student exchanges and religious groups, whose activities are hard to tell apart from legitimate charity, aid or cultural exchange. On variety of means, Liu describes a combined system of economic sanctions, political pressure, cultural infiltration and military force, with the internet and social media, in Liu's account, acting as a catalyst in Egypt, Tunisia and Iran.

Liu concludes that the US combines soft and hard methods in a mature system, and ties ideological unrest in the Middle East and Central Asia to "internet infiltration". The original title shows the piece is aimed at ideological education in Chinese universities. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese ideological-education scholarship framed US values diplomacy in 2015.
quoteEn: In many cases the US government does not always stand at the forefront of values export, but often uses non-governmental organisations, the media and religious groups to carry out its strategic intentions, which makes the practice highly concealed.
quoteZh: 在很多情况下，美国政府并不总是站在价值观输出的最前端，而往往假借非政府组织、媒体以及宗教团体来贯彻其战略意图，因而具有很强的隐蔽性。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese term for the deliberate promotion abroad of a state's political and ideological values. In Chinese ideological-security writing it usually describes US democracy promotion critically.
The idea that values such as liberal democracy and human rights apply to all societies. Chinese official and academic discourse often treats the concept as a vehicle for Western ideology.
The Chinese rendering of the US foreign-policy concept of combining hard and soft power, associated with the Obama administration.

t: Three paths to resolving the crisis of belief in Marxism
zh: 破解马克思主义信仰危机的三重路径
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2015, Xu Lan asks how to deal with what the author calls a crisis of belief in Marxism. Xu holds that Marxism still dominates China's ideological field, but is demonised on one side and turned into a utopia on the other. The article's answer is three linked paths, all concerned with Party conduct and discipline.

The piece opens by describing the crisis. Xu says it weakens the Party's cohesion and credibility and feeds social anxiety, hostility and utilitarianism. Xu lists causes: simplistic and dogmatic ideological education, pervasive corruption, early-rich groups who became vested interests, and wealth gaps that erode trust in government. Three sections then set out the remedies, and a short conclusion draws them together.

The first path treats Party integrity and the anti-corruption struggle as a matter of the survival of the Party and state. Xu argues that corruption stems from incomplete reform, not from reform itself, and calls for gradual institutional change, intra-Party supervision and public oversight, especially online. The second is full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, which Xu says must go beyond punishing corruption or running campaigns. It should set moral standards and forbidden zones, and value-building is described as a soft constraint alongside institutions. The third asks leading cadres, especially senior ones, to internalise political discipline and rules, with the revised Integrity Code and Disciplinary Regulations setting a moral "high line" and a disciplinary "bottom line". Xu also says cadres must take a clear stand against historical nihilism.

Xu concludes that these paths are ways of rebuilding belief in Marxism, and also support the modernization of state governance and the people's wellbeing. A healthy political life within the Party is presented as a basis for the free and comprehensive development of the individual. Read the original if you want a short example of how a 2015 Party journal tied ideological confidence to anti-corruption and discipline campaigns.
quoteEn: The key to resolving the crisis of belief lies with the Party.
quoteZh: 解决信仰危机，关键在党。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping, widely used since about 2014, for stricter discipline, anti-corruption work and ideological standards within the Communist Party.
In official Chinese usage, a label for views seen as distorting or negating the Party's history and socialist achievements.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: Firmly establishing the correct view of nationalities
zh: 牢固树立正确的民族观
paras: Writing in Qiushi in 2015, Hao Shiyuan sets out what the "correct view of nationalities" (minzuguan) means and why Chinese citizens should hold it. Taking Xi Jinping's remarks on ethnic work as the guiding text, Hao argues that this view rests on seeing the Chinese nation as a single, pluralistic-yet-unified family, and that building a shared spiritual home and a consciousness of the Chinese national community is the strategic task that follows.

The piece has two sections. The first defines the correct view of nationalities, sets it against Western experience with race and ethnicity, and states the basic policy orientation of Chinese ethnic work. The second turns to cultivating a consciousness of the Chinese national community, covering cultural identity, the two forms of nationalism to be opposed, and the place of ethnic work in state governance.

Hao distinguishes two senses of "nation": the modern state-nation (the Chinese nation) and the historical nationalities (the 56 groups) that compose it. In this account the Chinese nation is the only representative of China among the world's nations, and national unity is the precondition of state unity and territorial integrity. Hao presents Western policy as a long record of enslavement, segregation and forced assimilation. Multiculturalism, in this reading, has failed, citing Merkel's and Cameron's statements, the 2014 Ferguson unrest, a Council of Europe report and the Scottish and Catalan referendums. Against this, Hao describes the Chinese approach as respecting differences while narrowing gaps. This means a shared spiritual home and a shared material home, supported by common prosperity. Hao makes cultural identity the foundation. Chinese culture is not the same as Han culture but a synthesis of all groups' cultures, likened to an orchestra led by the Party with core socialist values as the main melody. Every group is said to carry the family surname "Chinese nation" along with its own given name. Narrow identification with one's own group breeds nationalism, which hostile forces can exploit, so Hao says the law and Party policy oppose both Han chauvinism and narrow local nationalism.

Hao concludes that ethnic work is part of modernizing the system and capacity of state governance. Its key is ethnic unity, and its most effective method is winning hearts. Persuasion grounded in respect for differences, together with bringing ethnic affairs fully under the rule of law, is how the correct view is to be established. Read the original if you want a concise, officially aligned statement of the Chinese Party-state's 2015 ethnic theory, including its critique of Western multiculturalism.
quoteEn: Every member of the pluralistic-yet-unified family bears the surname "Chinese nation" while each also has a given name of its own.
quoteZh: 多元一体大家庭的各个成员,都姓中华民族、同时各有其名。

glossary.explanation: The worldview applied to ethnic groups and ethnic questions. Official Chinese writing treats it as part of the superstructure and as a product of Marxism adapted to China.
A formula, associated with the anthropologist Fei Xiaotong, holding that the 56 ethnic groups form one Chinese nation. Official discourse presents it as a dialectical unity of the one and the many.

glossary.en: consciousness of the Chinese national community
glossary.literal: awareness of the Chinese nation as a community
glossary.explanation: A Party concept calling on all ethnic groups to identify first with the Chinese nation as a whole. It was prominent in Xi Jinping's ethnic policy discourse from 2014.
A phrase for the common cultural and ideological bonds among China's ethnic groups. Official texts pair it with a shared material home, meaning narrowing economic gaps.
The goal that all people share in the fruits of development. Here it is applied to narrowing gaps between ethnic regions and groups.

t: The influence of contemporary social trends of thought on young university students' thinking and behaviour, and how to guide it
zh: 当代社会思潮对青年大学生思想和行为的影响及其引导
paras: This article, posted in 2015 under ideological and political education, asks how contemporary social trends of thought (shehui sichao) affect the thinking and conduct of young university students, and how that influence should be guided. Zheng Jie and Ji Quansheng argue that students are especially open to such trends and that their ideological state will largely shape the future of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They conclude that guidance is needed at each stage in which students meet and use these ideas.

The article rests on a survey of 841 students, mostly from universities in Sichuan and Chongqing, with some respondents from 15 other provinces and regions. Of these, 551 were men, 290 women, and 530 studied sciences, engineering, agriculture or medicine. It first reports what students know about social trends of thought, then sets out positive and negative effects, and ends with proposals for guidance.

The survey finds shallow conceptual understanding: 51.01 per cent know the concept only a little, and 45.42 per cent cannot say whether Western ideological infiltration is a danger. Students most readily recognise money worship, individualism and democratic socialism. Books and newspapers (57.55 per cent) and classroom teaching (57.31 per cent) remain the main sources, with the internet third. The authors see positive effects in wider cultural horizons, more attention to real problems and stronger modern consciousness. They treat neoliberalism, democratic socialism and historical nihilism as the most harmful trends, claiming that they weaken faith in Marxism and in the socialist path, encourage individualism and multi-party ideas, and damage national self-respect.

Since the authors divide the spread of these ideas into contact, understanding and application, they propose guidance at three points. First, the internet should be both regulated and opened up: harmful sources blocked, sound explanatory material released to students, and specialist theory websites built, while Marxist propaganda continues. Second, universities should add history and culture courses and strengthen ideological and political theory teaching, including comparisons between Marxism and rival trends. Third, public opinion should be guided by praising positive conduct and condemning illegal or immoral acts, with the core socialist value system as the standard. Read the original if you want survey data on Chinese students' attitudes to social trends of thought, or an example of how such guidance is framed in 2015 ideological education.
quoteEn: We must change the former management mindset and model of simply "blocking": there must be blocking, but even more "channelling".
quoteZh: 要改变过去一味去“堵”的管理思维和管理模式，既要“堵”，更要“疏”。

glossary.explanation: Ideological currents that spread widely in society, such as neoliberalism or consumerism. In Chinese ideological work they are often assessed as to whether they challenge Marxism's guiding position.
A Western social-democratic current. Chinese official and academic writing often treats it as a rival ideology to Marxism.
A term in Chinese official discourse for views seen as distorting or negating the history of the revolution and of socialism in China.

glossary.zh: 社会主义核心价值体系
glossary.explanation: An official formulation of the basic values of Chinese socialism, with Marxism as its guiding thought. It was later replaced by the 'core socialist values'.

t: Challenges facing the Marxist view of journalism and strategies for responding
zh: 马克思主义新闻观面临的挑战及应对策略
paras: Writing in 2015, Liu Zuyu argues that the Marxist view of journalism faces a serious challenge in China's media sphere. In the author's account, a Western bourgeois view of journalism holds the discursive high ground in some outlets, while the Marxist view is marginalised. The core of the struggle, Liu says, is leadership of the media by the Party, which opponents contest under the banner of press freedom.

The article is a polemical commentary in two parts. The first describes the challenge: attacks on the Party principle in socialist media, the claim that the press is a "fourth power" or "public instrument", agenda-setting by online opinion leaders, the Southern Weekend incident of early 2013, and what Liu calls the hollowness of American press freedom. The second sets out four countermeasures, which the author offers as incomplete suggestions.

Liu contends that the Party's leadership of the media means the Party manages the media and the guidance of public opinion, and that content is "king" only when the guidance is correct. Agenda-setting, as Liu presents it, is the deliberate amplification of isolated negative incidents to erode the legitimacy of the ruling Party, and Liu says domestic and foreign hostile forces coordinate it. Citing Xi Jinping's 2013 remark that Western press freedom has ideological bottom lines, Liu treats press freedom as a tool for ideological infiltration. Liu also argues that calls for privately owned newspapers aim to open the way to political change.

Liu's proposals are these. The main official media should set their own agendas, rebut serious political rumours openly and keep control of public opinion. Internet management should be tightened. The journalist corps needs systematic Marxist training, and the political outlook of teachers in the 590 university journalism departments needs attention. Liu would also remove or retrain corrupt reporters and replace the economists and commentators who dominate media columns with Marxist scholars. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how the Marxist view of journalism was defended against liberal views of press freedom in the Chinese ideological debates of the early 2010s.
quoteEn: One point of endless contention in our public-opinion struggle with hostile forces at home and abroad is press freedom.
quoteZh: 我们和境内外敌对势力舆论战中的一个纠结不休的着重点就是新闻自由。

glossary.explanation: The official Chinese doctrine that journalism serves the Party and the people, and that media operate under Party leadership. It is taught in journalism education and contrasted with Western liberal press theory.
The official concept that media should steer public opinion in a direction consistent with Party and state priorities. Official texts treat it as a core task of Party-led media.
The principle that media must uphold the Party's line and accept its leadership. It is a core tenet of the Party's approach to the press.
A concept from Western communication studies, in which media shape which issues the public attends to. The author uses it for what is described as the deliberate hyping of negative incidents.

t: The social responsibility of Marxist theory workers
zh: 马克思主义理论工作者的社会责任
paras: Writing in 2015, Chen Xianda, a Marxist philosopher at Renmin University of China, asks what social responsibility university teachers in the humanities and social sciences bear, and in particular those who teach Marxist theory. His answer is that universities are a front line of ideological work and that teachers are the ones who must hold it, with both a sense of mission and the ability to carry it out.

The commentary begins with the idea that every occupation has its responsibilities, and cites Fichte's work on the vocation of the scholar. It then moves through the place of universities, the shared ideological task of all humanities and social science disciplines, the special position of the ideological and political theory courses, and the questions students raise in class about freedom, democracy, human rights and the rule of law.

Chen makes three main moves. First, he holds that every humanities and social science discipline has a guiding outlook (a view of history, of news, of literature and so on) and cannot be value-neutral. Marxism should guide these disciplines without replacing their specialist research, which should follow the 'Double Hundred' policy of free academic debate. Second, he argues that the ideological and political theory courses demand academic standards no lower than other courses. Teachers should not give students 'a bucket of water' but the ladle to draw it, meaning the ability to tell right from wrong, and should answer real social problems rather than recite slogans. Third, on freedom, democracy, human rights and the rule of law, he says no state can reject them, but their content depends on a country's social formation, economic level and cultural tradition. Teachers should therefore move beyond asking whether students want freedom to asking whose freedom and of what kind, and should reject the 'universal values' thesis and 'democracy export'.

Chen concludes that teachers need firm political qualities and real theoretical ability. He acknowledges past errors such as the Anti-Rightist campaign and the Cultural Revolution, and says progress in the rule of law has been made since reform and opening up and especially since the 18th Party Congress (2012). He also welcomes constructive criticism. He warns against people who smuggle private agendas into students' legitimate demands, and says patiently explaining these questions layer by layer is the theoretical responsibility of Marxist theory workers. Read the original if you want a senior Chinese philosopher's 2015 account of how Marxist teachers should handle ideological work and student questions about liberal values.
quoteEn: Responsibility is mission; ability is level of competence. Ability means being able to explain the reasoning clearly.
quoteZh: 责任是使命，能力是水平。所谓能力，就是要讲清道理。

glossary.explanation: A cultural and academic policy announced in 1956 encouraging free exchange of views in arts and sciences ('let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend'). It is invoked in official discourse to describe academic debate under Party guidance.
Compulsory Marxism-related courses taught to all Chinese university students, covering Marxism, Mao Zedong Thought and contemporary Chinese Marxism.
The idea that liberal values such as freedom, democracy and human rights apply equally everywhere. In Chinese official discourse the notion is often criticised as a vehicle for Western models.

t: Safeguarding national ideological security in the age of mobile networks
zh: 维护移动网络时代国家意识形态安全
paras: Writing in March 2015, Song Lidan argues that mobile networks (phones and tablets that combine mobile communication with the internet) have created a new and larger challenge to China's information and ideological security. In the author's account, as China's online climate improved after recent clean-up campaigns, "hostile forces" stepped up their infiltration and propaganda through mobile devices. The article's thesis is that mobile networks now have the capacity to affect national ideological security as a whole, and that the state must tighten regulation and strengthen positive propaganda in response.

The article has three parts. The first sets out why mobile networks matter, citing figures such as 875 million mobile network users in China by January 2015 and mobile phones as the main route onto the internet. The second identifies six categories of content on mobile social networks that the author says damage ideological security. The third turns to countermeasures, opening with US legislation on cyberspace and the 2011 US International Strategy for Cyberspace.

In explaining the threat, Song points to precisely targeted dissemination, the difficulty of controlling information on always-carried phones, the ability of small groups to amplify their voices (citing Moldova and Iran in 2009), and a user base weighted towards students, young people and lower-income groups. The author names WeChat and its "circle of friends" as a private space that avoids public transparency. The six categories include "exposés" rehabilitating landlords and discrediting heroes or Marx and Lenin; denigration of the Communist Party's role in the anti-Japanese war and rumours about the famine of 1959–61; claims that Chinese national character is poor because of the system; fabricated data on taxes, passports and incomes; demonisation of officials, teachers and urban management officers; and rumours after emergencies such as the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake.

Song calls for strengthened network supervision so that the state holds the "master switch" of network management, arguing that China should follow US and British practice and build matching laws and emergency mechanisms. The author also urges large-scale positive propaganda, the removal of offending public accounts, encouragement of accounts that spread "positive energy", research and publicity on national and Party history, and analysis of capitalism's essence and crises, in order to reinforce confidence in China's path, theory and system. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese scholar framed mobile internet governance as an ideological security issue in 2015.
quoteEn: Mobile networks have initially acquired the capacity to exert an overall influence on national information and ideological security.
quoteZh: 移动网络初步具备对国家信息与意识形态安全产生全局性影响的能力。

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese Party-state discourse referring to protecting the dominance of Marxism and the Party's official ideology against rival ideas. It is treated as part of national security.
A popular and official phrase for uplifting, officially approved content. Its counterpart, "negative energy" (负能量), denotes content seen as pessimistic or critical.
An official term for foreign or domestic actors presented as seeking to undermine the Party and the socialist system, usually without naming them.
A mobile messaging and social networking app launched by Tencent in 2011. Its "circle of friends" feature lets users share content with contacts they have added.

t: Cultivating and putting into practice core socialist values must start from the basics
zh: 培育践行社会主义核心价值观要从基础抓起
paras: Writing in 2015, Li Shenming takes up the 24-character core socialist values announced at the 18th Party Congress (2012) and argues that memorising them is easy, while cultivating and practising them is hard. His thesis is that practice, not mere knowledge, decides whether the values matter, and that it must be built up from a set of basic tasks. Without practice, he says, the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation "can only be a piece of empty paper".

The piece opens with Li's recollections of working in Zhongnanhai for over ten years, including accounts of Mao Zedong's austere living arrangements, and then moves through five numbered sections. These are: everyone is responsible; study and firm conviction; self-remoulding; leaders setting an example; and practising the values at all three levels (state, society, citizen). Li draws on a 2003 conversation with a Russian teacher in Volgograd, anecdotes about Mao and the revolutionary martyrs, and quotations from Marx and Engels, Xi Jinping and the Central Committee General Office's opinions on the values.

Li makes three main moves. First, he roots conviction in historical materialism: the people are the driving force of history, Marxism cannot be judged by short spans of time, and the martyrs' sacrifices show the strength of firm ideals. Second, he holds that values derive from the economic base, so they cannot be sustained by ideological education alone. In his view they require the basic economic system of the primary stage of socialism, with public ownership predominant and several forms of ownership developing together. Third, he rejects the view that human nature is selfish, calling it a product and defence of private ownership, and insists that officials must be consistent in word and deed, since their example is decisive. He cites the 2012 eight-point rules as evidence that leadership example works.

Li also answers three "misunderstandings": that freedom means doing as one pleases, that the values are merely capitalist or "universal" ones, and that those who practise them lose out. He holds that the prefix "socialist" changes their nature, and that law, policy and social justice must protect honest people. He ends by citing Mao's call to be "a noble person, a pure person", and urges that policies be brought into line with the values. Read the original if you want an example of how a senior Party theorist links core socialist values to Mao-era anecdotes, the economic base and the anti-corruption campaign.
quoteEn: Core socialist values cannot be cultivated and practised in the realm of ideas alone; nor can they be settled by \"ideological education\" by itself.
quoteZh: 社会主义核心价值观不可能仅仅是在观念领域培育践行，或者说不可能仅仅靠“思想教育”本身就能解决

glossary.explanation: A 24-character formula proposed at the 18th Party Congress in 2012, in three levels: state (prosperity, democracy, civility, harmony), society (freedom, equality, justice, rule of law) and citizen (patriotism, dedication, integrity, friendship).
A slogan associated with Xi Jinping from 2012, meaning the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
The official characterisation of China's present historical stage, used since the 1980s. It justifies a mixed economy with public ownership predominant.

t: Building "China's discursive power" from ideas and values
zh: 从思想和价值观上打造“中国话语权”
paras: Writing in 2015, Dai Mucai asks why China's economic rise, which made it the world's second-largest economy by 2010, has not yet produced matching influence in ideas. The author argues that Western discourse has largely supplied the intellectual and value framework for interpreting reform and opening up. Dai calls for building "China's discursive power" through original Chinese ideas, values and proposals, which the author treats as the core task of soft power.

The short commentary begins with this diagnosis: plenty of narration of achievements, but few Chinese ideas able to travel internationally. It then sets out what a new Chinese discourse system should contain, cites Xi Jinping's call to spread contemporary Chinese values, and discusses the conditions for intellectual innovation. It closes by linking the theme to think-tank building and the national rejuvenation goals.

Dai holds that soft power cannot rest on self-congratulatory language. The author says the discourse must draw on world civilisation, reflect China's distinctive culture, history and path, and show that path's significance for modernization and globalization. It must also creatively transform traditional culture. Dai describes innovation, inheritance and elimination as the three movements of cultural construction in an era of great change, with innovation the main theme, and expects clashes of views to be normal, as with the "hundred schools" and the Renaissance.

Dai names two conditions: thinkers and intellectuals should be the main agents of ideas, and the political and social environment should be tolerant and encouraging. The author sees the strategic task of building new-type think tanks with Chinese characteristics as opening space for this. Dai ties the matter to the "Four Comprehensives" and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese scholar in 2015 framed discursive power, soft power and think-tank building.
quoteEn: Without substantive content such as Chinese ideas, Chinese values and Chinese proposals, "Chinese discourse", "Chinese narration" and "the Chinese story" cannot move or persuade people or reach their hearts.
quoteZh: 没有中国思想、中国价值和中国主张等实质性内容，“中国话语”、“中国叙述”和“中国故事”就不可能打动人、说服人和走进人的心灵。

glossary.explanation: The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in 1978.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A long-term official goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, closely associated with the Chinese Dream.
A strategic framework put forward by Xi Jinping around 2014, covering a moderately prosperous society, deepening reform, governing according to law and strict Party governance.

glossary.en: new-type think tanks with Chinese characteristics
glossary.explanation: An official initiative, promoted from 2013 onwards, to develop policy research institutions serving Party and government decision-making.

t: Grasp the overall trend, focus on major tasks: doing ideological and publicity work in universities well under new circumstances
zh: 把握大势，着眼大事，努力做好新形势下高校宣传思想工作
paras: Yuan Guiren's article is a study-and-implementation commentary on the Opinions on Further Strengthening and Improving Publicity and Ideological Work in Universities under the New Circumstances, recently issued by the General Offices of the Party Central Committee and the State Council. Yuan presents the document as a programmatic text that carries out Xi Jinping's directives on ideological work. The article argues that implementing it is a major task for the education system, and that it requires clear understanding, concrete priorities and improved working methods.

The piece has three parts. The first explains why university ideological work matters. The second sets out four priority areas for action. The third lists four modes of thinking that officials should cultivate to raise their capacity. Yuan describes the situation in universities as basically healthy, citing 25 consecutive years of stability and the loyalty of most teachers and students. The article nonetheless warns of emerging tendencies that need close attention.

Yuan calls university ideological work a strategic, foundation-strengthening and soul-shaping project that bears on Party leadership and on whether socialism with Chinese characteristics has successors. The four priorities are: arming minds with theory and the core socialist values; managing ideological positions, including classrooms, textbooks, lectures and forums, and resisting what the author calls Western erroneous views and infiltration by hostile forces; building up the internet and mainstream opinion online; and strengthening the ranks of staff through Party committee responsibility and the training of Marxist talent. For capacity, Yuan calls for strategic, bottom-line, systems and rule-of-law thinking. The author identifies winning over young people as the fundamental problem, arguing that the greatest advantage of governing is winning youth and the greatest risk is losing them.

Yuan concludes that the Opinions must be put into effect through comprehensive, specific and workable plans, and not by merely answering documents with documents or going through the motions. The author also calls for better coordination among departments and for institutionalised, law-based handling of ideological problems on campus. Read the original if you want an official Ministry of Education-level account of how university ideological work was framed and prioritised in early 2015, including its stated concerns about the internet, textbooks and young people.
quoteEn: The most fundamental problem facing ideological work in universities today is how to win over young people.
quoteZh: 当前高校意识形态工作面临的最根本问题就是如何赢得青年。

glossary.explanation: A set of twenty-four characters in twelve values at the national, social and individual levels, formally promoted from the 18th Party Congress (2012). They are used as a basis for education and for building shared ideological ground.
Party and state activity to guide thought, shape public opinion and maintain the leading position of Marxism in culture, education and media.

t: The historical foundations of Marxist ideological discourse
zh: 马克思主义意识形态话语的历史基础
paras: Jiang Yingchun asks how Marx's critique of the German ideology equips readers to identify idealist accounts of history today. The article argues that Marx dismantled the idealist mode of historical cognition and built a materialist one, and that this critique supplies a method and criteria for spotting the overreach of ideas. Jiang contends that the idealist mode survives in contemporary scholarship, where some replace "history" with "narrative" and so deny history's objectivity and regularity.

The article is organised in three sections, drawing mainly on The German Ideology and The Poverty of Philosophy. The first asks why historical cognition is difficult. The second examines how ideological discourse becomes dependent on class rule. The third asks how the truth of ideology is revealed, through the contrast between false and genuine representatives of universal interests. Jiang repeatedly turns to the "farewell to revolution" thesis as a present-day example of idealist history.

Jiang's core argument has three moves. First, understanding history cannot rest on intuition or everyday experience, as Marx's shopkeeper analogy is meant to show. It requires the contradiction between productive forces and forms of intercourse, the formation of world history, and a rejection of abstract "man" and of the professional ideologist's faith in concepts. Second, since the ruling class controls the means of mental production, ruling ideas express ruling material relations, so any claim to a supra-class idea is illusory. Jiang concludes that all talk of "universal values" is a false theoretical claim. Third, every rising class presents its interest as universal, and ideology grows more moralised and sacralised as social contradictions sharpen. Jiang applies this to liberal economists who call capitalism "natural" and socialism "artificial", and to earlier minority revolutions. Only the proletariat, in Jiang's account, can unite class interest with universal interest.

Jiang concludes that the "farewell to revolution" thesis is a closed spiritual "system" that treats history as dough to be kneaded at will, reducing objective history to a history of ideas. Jiang reads it as claiming that Marxism's spread in China and the choice to take Russia as a model left the "mainstream of modern civilization". The author calls for this tendency to be overcome, warning of lasting harm in historical research. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar uses Marx's ideology critique against "universal values", historical nihilism and revisionist accounts of the Chinese revolution.
quoteEn: Marx scientifically explained the relation between the rule of ideas and class rule: the rule of ideas is an expression of class rule, and the so-called supremacy of ideas or of their rule does not exist.
quoteZh: 马克思科学说明了思想统治和阶级统治的关系，即思想统治是阶级统治的表现，所谓思想或思想统治的至上性是不存在的。
